status: COMPLETE DRAFT - independent academic review pending
method: Preserved 60-question Mock 01; extended each of Mocks 02-04 by 20 unused lecture-bank questions, balanced by lecture source and answer key; retained each original 40-question simulation.
online_source_role: OpenStax and NCBI resources used for concept triangulation; no external MCQ wording copied.

questions.stem: Why does the sinoatrial (SA) node normally determine the heart rate?
options: It is the only cardiac site that can generate impulses without nerve stimulation.
It reaches the threshold for spontaneous discharge sooner than other pacemakers.
It conducts electrical impulses through ventricular muscle faster than Purkinje fibres.
Its cells have a more negative resting membrane potential than ventricular cells.
It receives stronger sympathetic input than any other pacemaker tissue.
questions.explanation: The SA node has the highest normal intrinsic pacemaker rate. Its impulses reach subsidiary pacemakers before those slower sites discharge.
questions.distractor_note: Blood supply, contraction strength and ventricular conduction speed do not set the normal pacemaker hierarchy. Other conducting tissues also show automaticity.

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of slow impulse conduction through the AV node?
options: It allows the aortic valve to remain open during ventricular relaxation.
It allows atrial contraction to assist ventricular filling before ventricular systole.
It allows the pulmonary veins to contract before the atria fill.
It prevents the atria from depolarizing during every cardiac cycle.
It keeps ventricular contraction longer than ventricular relaxation at rest.
questions.explanation: The AV nodal delay separates atrial from ventricular activation so atrial systole can add blood to the ventricles before ventricular contraction starts.
questions.distractor_note: The AV delay coordinates atrial-to-ventricular timing; it does not set aortic valve opening, venous contraction or the resting systole-to-diastole ratio.

questions.stem: Left ventricular pressure has risen to 45 mmHg. Left atrial pressure is 10 mmHg and aortic pressure is 85 mmHg. Which phase is most likely?
options: Rapid ventricular filling
Reduced ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric relaxation
Rapid ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric contraction
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. The aortic valve remains closed because ventricular pressure is still below aortic pressure. Rising pressure with both valves closed indicates isovolumetric contraction.
questions.distractor_note: Ejection requires ventricular pressure above aortic pressure, while filling requires ventricular pressure below left atrial pressure.

questions.stem: Immediately after the aortic valve closes, left ventricular pressure begins to fall. Before the mitral valve opens, what happens to ventricular volume?
options: It increases quickly as blood enters from the atrium.
It increases slowly because the ventricle is relaxing.
It stays constant because both valves are closed.
It decreases quickly as blood leaves into the aorta.
It decreases slowly because the mitral valve leaks normally.
questions.explanation: After aortic valve closure and before mitral valve opening is isovolumetric relaxation. Pressure falls but neither inlet nor outlet is open, so ventricular volume remains unchanged.
questions.distractor_note: Filling starts only when the mitral valve opens; normal ejection ends when the aortic valve closes.

questions.chapter: CVS-02 / Pressure tracing and ejection onset
questions.stem: The diagram shows left ventricular pressure (solid) and aortic pressure (dashed). At which labelled point does aortic valve opening begin?
options: Point B
Point A
Point C
Point D
Point E
questions.explanation: The aortic valve opens as rising left ventricular pressure first exceeds aortic pressure. On the plotted curves this happens at B. Point A precedes the pressure crossover; C and D occur later in ejection, and E follows valve closure.
questions.distractor_note: All other labels are placed before or after the initial ventricular-aortic pressure crossover.

questions.chapter: CVS-02 / Stroke volume and ejection fraction
questions.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL and an end-systolic volume of 56 mL. What is its ejection fraction?
questions.explanation: Stroke volume = 140 - 56 = 84 mL. Ejection fraction = (84/140) x 100 = 60%.
questions.distractor_note: 84 mL is the stroke volume, not a percentage; 40% is the fraction remaining after systole.

questions.stem: A pulse is felt at the wrist after the left ventricle ejects blood. What travels along the arteries to produce this pulse?
options: The same column of blood moving from the aorta to the wrist within one beat
A contraction wave moving through arterial smooth muscle
A wave of ventricular electrical activity passing along the artery
A pressure wave that expands the arterial wall
A pulse of venous pressure transmitted backward into the radial artery
questions.explanation: Ventricular ejection generates a pressure wave that travels through elastic arteries and briefly expands their walls. The wave travels faster than the average blood itself.
questions.distractor_note: The palpable pulse is pressure-wave transmission, not blood velocity or an electrical impulse.

questions.stem: In complete AV dissociation, an atrium sometimes contracts while the tricuspid valve is closed. Which jugular venous finding may appear?
options: A persistently absent a wave
Intermittent giant v waves caused by atrial systole
Loss of the y descent with every normal beat
A regular arterial-type pulse in the jugular vein
Intermittent giant a waves
questions.explanation: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve causes a sudden large rise in right atrial pressure, producing cannon or giant a waves.
questions.distractor_note: The a wave reflects atrial contraction; the v wave mainly reflects atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed.

questions.stem: Why does inspiration normally widen the split between the aortic and pulmonary components of the second heart sound?
options: Increased right ventricular filling delays mitral valve opening.
Increased right ventricular filling delays pulmonary valve closure.
Reduced right ventricular filling delays aortic valve closure.
Increased left ventricular filling delays tricuspid valve closure.
Reduced left ventricular filling delays the first heart sound.
questions.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, often prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying P2 relative to A2.
questions.distractor_note: S2 reflects semilunar valve closure, not AV valve opening or closure.

questions.stem: A patient has backward blood flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole. Which valve disorder best explains this?
options: Mitral stenosis
Aortic stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation
questions.explanation: Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve fails to prevent systolic backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
questions.distractor_note: Mitral stenosis obstructs diastolic forward flow; aortic disorders affect flow across the aortic valve, and tricuspid regurgitation affects the right heart.

questions.stem: A third heart sound (S3) is heard shortly after S2. With which part of the cardiac cycle is it associated?
options: Atrial contraction just before S1
Isovolumetric ventricular contraction
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Rapid ventricular filling
Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves
questions.explanation: S3 is associated with rapid early-diastolic ventricular filling and the resulting vibrations. It may be physiological in young people but can be abnormal in older patients.
questions.distractor_note: S4 is associated with late-diastolic atrial contraction; S1 and S2 correspond to valve closure events.

questions.stem: Venous return rises while heart rate, afterload and contractility remain unchanged. What immediate change is expected in a normal ventricle?
options: A rise in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A fall in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A rise in stroke volume with a fall in end-diastolic volume
A fall in stroke volume despite a rise in end-diastolic volume
No change in stroke volume despite greater ventricular filling
questions.explanation: More venous return increases ventricular filling and stretches cardiac fibres. On the ascending Frank-Starling relationship this raises force and stroke volume.
questions.distractor_note: The Frank-Starling response links greater preload to greater output within physiological limits.

questions.stem: Aortic pressure suddenly rises. For the first affected beat, ventricular filling and contractility are unchanged. What is the likely effect on stroke volume?
options: Stroke volume increases because aortic recoil becomes stronger.
Stroke volume increases because ventricular filling has increased.
Stroke volume stays constant because heart rate has not changed.
Stroke volume decreases because the ventricle ejects against greater pressure.
Stroke volume increases because the AV node conducts more quickly.
questions.explanation: Greater afterload makes ventricular ejection more difficult. Before compensatory adjustments, end-systolic volume tends to increase and stroke volume decreases.
questions.distractor_note: Aortic recoil, filling and AV conduction are not the mechanisms determining the first-beat afterload response.

questions.chapter: CVS-05 / Contractility and ventricular function curve
questions.stem: Two ventricular function curves are shown. At the same end-diastolic volume, curve X produces a larger stroke volume than curve Y. What best explains the difference?
options: Ventricular preload must be greater on curve X.
The heart rate must be lower on curve X.
The aortic valve must be closed throughout ejection on curve X.
The ventricular muscle must be less responsive to calcium on curve X.
Ventricular contractility is greater on curve X.
questions.explanation: An upward shift of the Frank-Starling curve indicates greater stroke volume at the same preload, consistent with increased contractility.
questions.distractor_note: The comparison holds end-diastolic volume constant, so increased preload is not the explanation; reduced calcium response would tend to reduce contractility.

questions.chapter: CVS-05 / Heart rate and filling time
questions.stem: At a very fast heart rate, stroke volume may fall even when the heart contracts strongly. What is the main reason?
options: Systole disappears as heart rate rises.
Atrial contraction stops whenever the heart rate exceeds normal.
The semilunar valves remain open throughout the next beat.
The ventricles lose all ability to contract when diastole shortens.
Diastole becomes too short for adequate ventricular filling.
questions.explanation: As heart rate rises substantially, diastole shortens disproportionately. Reduced filling time can lower end-diastolic volume and hence stroke volume.
questions.distractor_note: Tachycardia does not abolish systole or automatically stop atrial contraction; the main issue is reduced filling time.

questions.stem: Oxygen consumption is 280 mL/min. Arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous oxygen content is 130 mL/L. What is cardiac output?
options: 4 L/min
2 L/min
3 L/min
5 L/min
7 L/min
questions.explanation: Arterial-mixed venous oxygen content difference = 200 - 130 = 70 mL/L. Cardiac output = 280 mL/min divided by 70 mL/L = 4 L/min.
questions.distractor_note: The Fick method divides oxygen consumption by the oxygen content difference, not by either concentration alone.

questions.stem: For cardiac output measurement using the oxygen Fick principle, why is blood sampled from the pulmonary artery?
options: It contains mixed venous blood returning from the systemic circulation.
It contains freshly oxygenated blood leaving the lungs.
It measures oxygen content in the coronary arteries only.
It has the same oxygen content as any single peripheral vein.
It directly measures left ventricular stroke volume without a calculation.
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries a mixture of venous returns from systemic tissues before oxygenation in the lungs. A single peripheral vein does not represent the whole-body mixed venous oxygen content.
questions.distractor_note: A pulmonary artery sample is mixed venous, not systemic arterial blood or a direct stroke-volume measurement.

questions.chapter: CVS-06 / Pressure work and oxygen demand
questions.stem: At the same stroke volume and heart rate, which change generally increases myocardial oxygen demand more?
options: Pumping against a lower arterial pressure
Reducing the pressure needed to open the aortic valve
Pumping against a much higher arterial pressure
Lowering wall tension during ventricular ejection
Reducing the pressure difference across the aortic valve
questions.explanation: Pressure work, which increases with afterload and myocardial wall tension, carries a high oxygen cost. Pumping the same volume against greater arterial pressure is more demanding.
questions.distractor_note: The alternative changes reduce pressure load rather than increase it.

questions.stem: According to Poiseuille's law, if a vessel radius is reduced to half while other factors remain constant, how does resistance change?
options: It becomes 2 times greater.
It becomes 4 times greater.
It becomes 16 times greater.
It becomes 8 times greater.
It becomes 16 times smaller.
questions.explanation: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Halving radius therefore increases resistance by 2^4 = 16 times.
questions.distractor_note: The fourth-power dependence is stronger than a linear, square or cubic change.

questions.chapter: CVS-07 / Flow velocity and cross-sectional area
questions.stem: Why is average blood-flow velocity normally much lower in capillaries than in the aorta?
options: The total capillary cross-sectional area is smaller than that of the aorta.
Capillaries receive a smaller total blood flow than the aorta in steady state.
Capillary pressure is lower, so red cells are stationary between heartbeats.
The combined cross-sectional area of all capillaries is much larger.
Blood viscosity is so much higher in capillaries that flow velocity must be zero.
questions.explanation: For a given volume flow rate, average velocity equals flow divided by cross-sectional area. The enormous total capillary area produces low average velocity.
questions.distractor_note: Flow continues in capillaries; the key comparison is total cross-sectional area, not the diameter of one capillary.

questions.stem: A patient develops marked polycythaemia. If vascular diameter and pressure gradient are otherwise unchanged, what happens to resistance?
options: It decreases because blood viscosity increases.
It decreases because plasma oncotic pressure rises.
It stays unchanged because haematocrit affects oxygen only.
It stays unchanged because viscosity influences velocity but not flow resistance.
It increases because blood viscosity increases.
questions.explanation: A higher red-cell concentration generally increases blood viscosity. Greater viscosity increases resistance to flow under otherwise similar conditions.
questions.distractor_note: Haematocrit affects blood rheology as well as oxygen carriage.

questions.stem: Which isolated change increases the tendency for turbulent flow in a blood vessel?
options: An increase in blood viscosity
A decrease in blood density
An increase in blood-flow velocity
A decrease in vessel diameter
A decrease in the Reynolds number
questions.explanation: Reynolds number increases with velocity, density and diameter, and decreases with viscosity. Increased velocity therefore makes turbulence more likely.
questions.distractor_note: Higher viscosity and smaller diameter generally lower Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.

questions.stem: An electromagnetic blood-flow meter estimates flow by measuring what happens when blood moves through a magnetic field. What does it detect?
options: The oxygen consumed by blood during each passage
The sound produced when the blood becomes turbulent
An electrical voltage induced across the moving blood
The amount of plasma protein filtered into tissues
The pressure required to close a sphygmomanometer cuff
questions.explanation: Moving conducting blood through a magnetic field generates a voltage. The signal can be related to blood-flow velocity and hence flow under the meter's calibrated conditions.
questions.distractor_note: Oxygen consumption, Korotkoff sounds and filtration are separate measurement concepts.

questions.stem: A resting adult has a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg. Using the usual resting approximation, what is mean arterial pressure?
options: 75 mmHg
90 mmHg
85 mmHg
95 mmHg
105 mmHg
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = 120 - 75 = 45 mmHg. MAP is approximately diastolic pressure + one-third of pulse pressure = 75 + 15 = 90 mmHg.
questions.distractor_note: MAP is not the simple arithmetic midpoint; diastole usually occupies more time at rest.

questions.stem: In a healthy adult, cuff pressure is slowly released during blood-pressure measurement. Disappearance of Korotkoff sounds usually marks which pressure?
options: Systolic arterial pressure
Mean arterial pressure
Diastolic arterial pressure
Pulse pressure
Central venous pressure
questions.explanation: As cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the brachial artery is open throughout the cardiac cycle and the characteristic Korotkoff sounds generally disappear.
questions.distractor_note: The first appearance of sound usually marks systolic rather than diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: What helps maintain arterial blood flow during ventricular diastole, when the left ventricle is not ejecting?
options: Persistent ejection by the ventricle after the aortic valve closes
Elastic recoil of arteries stretched during systole
Active contraction of the aortic valve leaflets during diastole
Pressure transmitted from the right ventricle into the aorta
The skeletal muscle pump acting directly on the ascending aorta
questions.explanation: The aorta and large elastic arteries store energy during systole and release it as they recoil in diastole, helping maintain downstream pressure and flow.
questions.distractor_note: Valve cusps prevent backflow but do not actively generate forward arterial pressure.

questions.stem: A deep vein in one leg becomes obstructed, increasing pressure in vessels upstream. What local change most directly favours swelling?
options: An increase in plasma albumin concentration
A decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure
An increase in lymphatic drainage capacity
A decrease in capillary wall permeability
An increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.explanation: Impaired venous drainage raises capillary pressure and promotes movement of fluid from capillaries into interstitial tissue.
questions.distractor_note: Higher plasma oncotic pressure or stronger lymphatic removal would oppose fluid accumulation.

questions.stem: A patient has very low plasma albumin but unchanged capillary blood pressure. Why can oedema develop?
options: The plasma colloid osmotic force drawing fluid into vessels increases.
The permeability of capillaries to water decreases throughout the body.
The capillary hydrostatic pressure decreases enough to prevent filtration.
The osmotic force retaining water within the circulation is reduced.
Lymphatic return increases enough to oppose all local filtration.
questions.explanation: Albumin contributes strongly to plasma colloid osmotic pressure. Less albumin weakens the opposing force to filtration, promoting net tissue fluid accumulation.
questions.distractor_note: Low albumin affects oncotic pressure; it does not abolish hydrostatic pressure or convert lymph into plasma.

questions.stem: A patient develops chronic swelling of an arm after axillary lymph nodes are removed. What is the main reason?
options: Arterial blood supply to the arm has completely stopped.
Red blood cells begin moving freely out of intact capillaries.
The heart pumps excess blood only into the affected arm.
Interstitial fluid and proteins cannot drain normally through lymph vessels.
Plasma albumin production increases sharply in the affected tissue.
questions.explanation: Damage to lymphatic pathways reduces the return of interstitial fluid and proteins to the blood, producing lymphoedema.
questions.distractor_note: Lymphoedema is caused by impaired lymph removal, not complete loss of arterial flow.

questions.stem: Why does walking help return blood from the leg veins to the heart?
options: Muscle contractions compress veins while valves limit backward flow.
Venous valves in the calf actively push blood toward the heart.
Walking lowers all leg capillary pressures to zero.
Muscle compression pushes venous blood toward the feet through open valves.
Veins become less compliant and no longer experience gravity.
questions.explanation: Contraction of leg muscles compresses nearby veins. One-way venous valves direct the displaced blood centrally, limiting pooling.
questions.distractor_note: Venous valves are passive one-way structures; muscle compression supplies the pumping action.

questions.stem: During exercise, working skeletal muscle produces more CO2, H+ and other metabolites. What local vascular response is expected?
options: Arteriolar constriction that reduces supply to active muscle
Arteriolar dilation that increases blood supply to the active muscle
Closure of all capillaries until the exercise finishes
A reduction in local flow despite increased oxygen demand
Selective closure of venous valves inside the muscle
questions.explanation: Local metabolic vasodilators help match perfusion to greater tissue metabolic activity. Dilation reduces resistance and permits more flow.
questions.distractor_note: Active tissue usually needs greater, not lower, local perfusion.

questions.stem: Pressure inside a small artery suddenly rises. What initial response of its smooth muscle helps resist the increase in flow?
options: It relaxes in response to the extra stretch.
It maintains the same diameter while pressure rises.
It contracts in response to the extra stretch.
It dilates because greater pressure directly lowers smooth-muscle calcium entry.
It dilates because its oxygen requirement falls whenever pressure increases.
questions.explanation: Myogenic autoregulation means that increased transmural pressure stretches vascular smooth muscle, which contracts and raises resistance.
questions.distractor_note: A myogenic response differs from metabolic vasodilation caused by increased tissue activity.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a forearm artery is briefly blocked and then restored. Why may flow temporarily rise above its resting level?
options: Vasodilator metabolites built up while the tissue was underperfused.
The heart has permanently increased the forearm's blood supply.
The arterial pulse wave has stopped travelling through the arm.
The blockage permanently removed vascular resistance.
Venous valves now actively force arterial blood toward the hand.
questions.explanation: During the occlusion, tissue oxygen delivery falls and local vasodilatory signals build up. When flow resumes, dilated resistance vessels produce transient reactive hyperaemia.
questions.distractor_note: Reactive hyperaemia is a temporary local response to preceding flow interruption.

questions.stem: The graph shows blood flow across a range of perfusion pressures. Between points B and C, why is flow nearly constant despite rising pressure?
options: Arteriolar resistance falls as perfusion pressure rises.
Cardiac output stops changing throughout the entire body.
Arteriolar resistance rises as perfusion pressure rises.
Venous blood begins flowing backward into the artery.
The tissue stops consuming oxygen over this pressure range.
questions.explanation: For approximately constant flow Q, a higher perfusion pressure requires a higher local resistance (Q = pressure difference / resistance). The plateau reflects autoregulatory adjustment.
questions.distractor_note: Falling resistance alongside increasing pressure would increase, rather than stabilize, flow.

questions.chapter: CVS-11 / Baroreceptor reflex fall in BP
questions.stem: A person suddenly loses blood and arterial pressure falls. Which immediate autonomic change helps restore pressure?
options: Reduced sympathetic activity and increased vagal activity
Reduced sympathetic and reduced vagal activity together
Increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal activity
Increased vagal activity with arteriolar dilation
No change in autonomic outflow until blood volume recovers
questions.explanation: Less stretch of carotid and aortic baroreceptors reduces afferent firing. The medulla responds with increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic outflow.
questions.distractor_note: Increased vagal activity would tend to slow the heart rather than compensate for falling pressure.

questions.chapter: CVS-11 / Baroreceptor reflex rise in BP
questions.stem: Arterial pressure suddenly increases. What happens to the rate of firing of carotid sinus baroreceptors?
options: It decreases because the arterial wall is stretched more.
It stops because baroreceptors respond only to falling pressure.
It increases because the arterial wall is stretched more.
It becomes independent of stretch and depends only on blood oxygen.
It is replaced completely by discharge from the carotid body chemoreceptors.
questions.explanation: Carotid sinus baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive. Increased arterial pressure increases wall distension and afferent firing, contributing to reflex bradycardia and vasodilation.
questions.distractor_note: Baroreceptors respond to pressure-related stretch; carotid bodies are distinct chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: A patient develops rapidly rising intracranial pressure with impaired brainstem perfusion. Which combination is typical of the Cushing response?
options: Increased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Decreased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Increased arterial pressure with sustained reflex tachycardia
Decreased arterial pressure with complete loss of sympathetic tone
Unchanged arterial pressure with marked peripheral vasodilation
questions.explanation: Reduced medullary perfusion causes a powerful sympathetic rise in systemic pressure. The resulting arterial hypertension stimulates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia.
questions.distractor_note: The raised pressure is a compensatory response to brainstem ischemia; bradycardia is secondary to the baroreflex.

questions.stem: Rapid infusion of fluid increases venous return and stretches the right atrium. Which reflex response may help accommodate the larger venous return?
options: Heart rate may decrease because atrial stretch directly increases vagal outflow.
Heart rate may increase as atrial stretch activates a reflex.
Heart rate may remain unchanged because atrial stretch has no reflex effects.
Heart rate may decrease because venous return is reduced by the fluid infusion.
Heart rate may increase only if the arterial baroreceptors first detect hypotension.
questions.explanation: The atrial stretch (Bainbridge) reflex can increase heart rate when venous return and atrial filling rise. It is distinct from the arterial baroreceptor response to elevated blood pressure.
questions.distractor_note: Atrial distension can elicit reflex tachycardia without requiring arterial hypotension. The infusion increases rather than reduces venous return.

questions.stem: Immediately after a person stands up quickly, before reflex compensation has fully developed, what tends to happen?
options: Venous pooling decreases and ventricular filling rises.
Venous pooling increases and venous return to the heart falls.
Venous pressure in the feet falls below pressure at heart level.
Cardiac output rises because gravity pushes blood toward the chest.
Cerebral blood flow increases because the head is now above the heart.
questions.explanation: Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure and pooling in dependent veins. This reduces central venous return, initially lowering stroke volume and potentially cerebral perfusion.
questions.distractor_note: Without compensation, standing does not drive leg blood centrally or raise head-level perfusion.

questions.stem: Why can sustained head-to-foot acceleration (+Gz) cause a pilot to lose consciousness?
options: Blood shifts toward the legs, reducing pressure and flow to the brain.
Blood shifts toward the head, causing cerebral venous congestion.
Pulmonary artery pressure becomes identical to aortic pressure.
The cardiac conducting system stops generating electrical impulses.
Cerebral arteries are forced to dilate without any change in perfusion.
questions.explanation: Positive G increases the hydrostatic pressure gradient toward the lower body, encouraging dependent pooling and reducing cerebral arterial perfusion.
questions.distractor_note: Headward blood shifts and facial congestion are characteristic of negative rather than positive head-to-foot G.

questions.stem: A person loses a substantial amount of blood. What sequence most directly explains the initial fall in cardiac output?
options: Lower blood volume directly raises ventricular end-diastolic volume.
Lower blood volume immediately increases plasma oncotic pressure enough to raise output.
Lower blood volume causes the aortic valve to open earlier at a higher stroke volume.
Lower blood volume leads to lower venous return and ventricular filling.
Lower blood volume raises pulmonary venous return above systemic venous return.
questions.explanation: Blood loss reduces circulating volume and venous return, which reduces preload and stroke volume. Reflex vasoconstriction may defend pressure but cannot automatically restore lost flow.
questions.distractor_note: Loss of circulating volume does not directly raise preload or stroke volume.

questions.stem: A patient with severe infection has widespread arteriolar dilation and low arterial pressure. Which shock mechanism is most likely?
options: Hypovolaemic shock caused mainly by external blood loss
Cardiogenic shock caused mainly by poor ventricular pumping
Obstructive shock caused mainly by mechanical blockage of blood flow
A normal circulation with a temporary rise in vascular resistance
Distributive shock caused mainly by reduced systemic vascular resistance
questions.explanation: Sepsis can produce profound vasodilation and loss of vascular tone, lowering total peripheral resistance and effective perfusion pressure. This is distributive shock.
questions.distractor_note: The defining event in this stem is widespread low resistance rather than haemorrhage, pump failure or obstruction.

questions.stem: During prolonged severe shock, lactic acidosis worsens and the circulation becomes less responsive to catecholamines. What may happen next?
options: Tissue oxygen delivery automatically returns to normal.
Systemic vascular resistance must remain high indefinitely.
Myocardial function improves because acid increases calcium sensitivity.
Vascular tone and cardiac performance can deteriorate further.
Renal blood flow becomes independent of arterial pressure.
questions.explanation: Poor tissue perfusion drives anaerobic metabolism and acidosis. Acidosis and ischemia can depress myocardial function and vascular responses, creating a vicious cycle.
questions.distractor_note: Decompensated shock may overwhelm compensatory mechanisms; hypoxia and acidosis do not reliably improve pump function.

questions.stem: A patient with left ventricular failure develops breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. What pressure change most directly promotes fluid movement into the lungs?
options: Increased pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure
Decreased pulmonary venous pressure
Increased plasma oncotic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Decreased hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Increased lymphatic drainage with unchanged capillary pressure
questions.explanation: Poor left ventricular output raises pressure upstream in the left atrium and pulmonary veins. Higher pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes filtration and pulmonary oedema.
questions.distractor_note: Fluid filtration increases with raised hydrostatic pressure; higher oncotic pressure would tend to oppose it.

questions.stem: A student faints after seeing a frightening injury. Immediately before fainting, which combination is most consistent with a vasovagal episode?
options: Increased heart rate and widespread vasoconstriction
Increased heart rate with marked skeletal-muscle vasoconstriction only
Unchanged heart rate with increased cardiac contractility
Increased blood volume and increased venous return
Reduced heart rate and widespread vasodilation
questions.explanation: Vasovagal syncope commonly involves increased vagal influence and reduced sympathetic vascular tone, resulting in bradycardia and vasodilation that reduce cerebral perfusion.
questions.distractor_note: The combined fall in heart rate and vascular resistance distinguishes the typical vasovagal response from compensatory sympathetic activation.

questions.stem: An obstruction mainly affects blood supply to the lateral surface of a cerebral hemisphere. Which major cerebral artery is most likely involved?
options: Anterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Anterior communicating artery
Middle cerebral artery
Basilar artery
questions.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies much of the lateral cerebral hemisphere. The anterior cerebral artery supplies much of the medial frontal and parietal surface.
questions.distractor_note: The anterior and posterior cerebral arteries supply other major territories; communicating arteries are chiefly connectors in the arterial circle.

questions.stem: The cerebral aqueduct becomes blocked while CSF production continues. Which ventricles are expected to enlarge first?
options: The fourth ventricle alone
The third and fourth ventricles only
The lateral ventricles and fourth ventricle only
The lateral and third ventricles
The fourth ventricle and central canal only
questions.explanation: The aqueduct links the third to the fourth ventricle. Obstruction causes CSF to accumulate upstream in the third and lateral ventricles.
questions.distractor_note: The fourth ventricle lies downstream of the aqueduct and is not the primary site of enlargement in an isolated aqueduct blockage.

questions.stem: Brain capillary endothelial cells have tight junctions. How does glucose normally cross into brain tissue?
options: By moving freely between endothelial cells despite their tight junctions
By passing directly through membrane lipid without any carrier
By crossing endothelial ion channels that transport sodium and potassium
By passing from plasma to astrocytes without crossing the capillary endothelium
Through specific glucose transport proteins in the endothelial membrane
questions.explanation: The blood-brain barrier restricts paracellular movement, but glucose is carried across endothelial membranes by transporters such as GLUT1.
questions.distractor_note: Glucose does not normally pass freely between tightly joined endothelial cells.

questions.stem: Mean arterial pressure is 95 mmHg and intracranial pressure is 15 mmHg. Assuming cerebral venous pressure is not higher than intracranial pressure, what is cerebral perfusion pressure?
options: 65 mmHg
75 mmHg
80 mmHg
95 mmHg
110 mmHg
questions.explanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is approximately MAP - ICP when ICP is the effective downstream pressure: 95 - 15 = 80 mmHg.
questions.distractor_note: Perfusion pressure is a difference between driving and downstream pressures; it is not the MAP alone.

questions.stem: Why does most left ventricular coronary blood flow occur during diastole rather than systole?
options: The left coronary artery is closed by the aortic valve during systole.
Blood in coronary arteries contains oxygen only during diastole.
The heart stops using oxygen during systole.
Pulmonary venous pressure becomes higher than aortic pressure during systole.
Contracting left ventricular muscle compresses vessels within its wall.
questions.explanation: During left ventricular systole, high intramyocardial pressure compresses coronary vessels, especially in the subendocardium. Relaxation during diastole permits better perfusion.
questions.distractor_note: Coronary arterial openings remain connected to the aorta; the critical factor is compression by contracting myocardium.

questions.stem: A region of heart muscle works harder and uses more oxygen. Which local change helps increase coronary blood flow?
options: Build-up of metabolites such as adenosine promotes arteriolar dilation.
Reduced metabolic activity causes arteriolar dilation in that region.
Increased oxygen extraction alone is always sufficient at any workload.
Aortic pressure becomes independent of coronary vessel resistance.
Increased adenosine produces sustained constriction of the local coronary arterioles.
questions.explanation: The myocardium already extracts much of the oxygen from coronary blood at rest. Higher demand is met largely by increased coronary flow, partly driven by metabolic vasodilators such as adenosine.
questions.distractor_note: Coronary metabolic regulation increases flow in active muscle; adenosine is a vasodilator in this setting.

questions.stem: One group of alveoli is poorly ventilated while nearby alveoli are well ventilated. What happens to the small pulmonary arteries supplying the poorly ventilated region?
options: They dilate, directing more blood toward the poorly ventilated alveoli.
They remain unchanged because oxygen never affects pulmonary resistance.
They constrict only if systemic arterial pressure is also high.
They close because all pulmonary arteries normally lack smooth muscle.
They constrict, directing more blood toward better-ventilated alveoli.
questions.explanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary arteriolar constriction. This helps divert flow toward alveoli where oxygen uptake is more effective.
questions.distractor_note: The pulmonary hypoxic response is opposite to the usual local hypoxic vasodilation in systemic tissues.

questions.stem: During exercise, pulmonary blood flow increases greatly but pulmonary arterial pressure rises relatively little. What helps explain this?
options: Most pulmonary capillaries close as flow increases.
Previously underperfused capillaries open and existing vessels widen.
Pulmonary vascular resistance increases in direct proportion to flow.
The right ventricle stops pumping blood during exercise.
The alveoli stop exchanging gases while blood flow rises.
questions.explanation: Recruitment of additional pulmonary capillaries and distension of vessels increase the total flow capacity, limiting the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure.
questions.distractor_note: Recruitment and distension expand, not reduce, pulmonary vascular capacity.

questions.stem: During severe haemorrhage, sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the gut. What is one immediate benefit of this response?
options: It increases digestion by delivering more blood to intestinal villi.
It helps preserve perfusion pressure for vital organs by reducing splanchnic flow.
It prevents any reduction in cardiac output regardless of blood loss.
It sends all oxygenated blood directly into the hepatic portal vein.
It permanently prevents ischemic damage to the intestinal mucosa.
questions.explanation: The splanchnic bed is a large vascular reservoir. Sympathetic constriction can redistribute blood and support systemic pressure during shock, although prolonged gut ischemia can be harmful.
questions.distractor_note: Reduced splanchnic flow supports central circulation but does not guarantee normal cardiac output or prevent gut ischemia.

questions.stem: After firm stroking of the skin, redness spreads beyond the directly stimulated line. What produces this surrounding flare?
options: An axon reflex causing nearby arterioles to dilate
Clotting of capillaries at the site of injury
A sudden fall in total circulating blood volume
Closure of all precapillary sphincters around the area
Direct filtration of red blood cells into the epidermis
questions.explanation: The flare of the triple response is produced by an antidromic axon reflex that dilates vessels around the stimulated region.
questions.distractor_note: The wheal reflects increased local permeability, whereas the flare is spreading arteriolar vasodilation.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin binds oxygen more strongly than adult haemoglobin under comparable conditions. Which property contributes to this difference?
options: Local fluid filtration that forms the raised wheal
Dilation restricted to vessels directly under the stroked line
Reflex withdrawal of sympathetic tone from the entire skin circulation
Venous congestion caused by pressure on deep veins beneath the skin
Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG less strongly.
questions.explanation: The lower affinity of fetal haemoglobin for 2,3-BPG contributes to its higher oxygen affinity, supporting oxygen transfer across the placenta.
questions.distractor_note: Fetal haemoglobin still unloads oxygen to tissues; it simply has a left-shifted dissociation curve compared with adult haemoglobin.

questions.stem: What change occurs in the pulmonary circulation with the newborn's first breaths?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises as alveolar oxygen rises.
Pulmonary blood flow stops because placental blood flow has ended.
Pulmonary vascular resistance falls as the lungs expand and oxygen rises.
The ductus venosus begins carrying blood from the right ventricle.
Systemic vascular resistance falls because the placenta remains connected.
questions.explanation: Lung expansion and increased alveolar oxygen reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, raising pulmonary blood flow. Loss of the placenta simultaneously tends to raise systemic vascular resistance.
questions.distractor_note: The first breaths promote pulmonary vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Which pair of electrodes forms standard bipolar lead I in an ECG?
options: Right arm (negative) and left leg (positive)
Left arm (negative) and left leg (positive)
Left leg (negative) and right arm (positive)
Right arm (negative) and left arm (positive)
Left arm (negative) and right arm (positive)
questions.explanation: Standard lead I measures the potential difference LA(+) minus RA(-). Lead II uses RA(-) and LL(+), while lead III uses LA(-) and LL(+).
questions.distractor_note: Lead II and III use the left-leg electrode; reversing the lead I polarity is also incorrect.

questions.stem: An ECG has a PR interval of 0.24 seconds, with a normal-width QRS complex and every P wave followed by a QRS. What does this pattern indicate?
options: First-degree AV block (prolonged AV conduction)
Complete AV block with no atrioventricular conduction
A shortened PR interval with normal conduction
Ventricular fibrillation with absent organised QRS complexes
Atrial fibrillation with irregular atrial activation
questions.explanation: A PR interval longer than 0.20 s with one-to-one AV conduction is first-degree AV block. The normal-width QRS is compatible with delayed AV conduction without loss of beats.
questions.distractor_note: Complete AV block requires loss of consistent P-to-QRS conduction; atrial fibrillation has no regular organised P waves.

questions.stem: In the ECG strip, the distance between consecutive R waves is 20 small squares. The paper speed is 25 mm/s. What is the heart rate?
options: 60 beats/min
75 beats/min
80 beats/min
100 beats/min
120 beats/min
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, one small square = 0.04 s. Twenty squares = 0.8 s per beat, giving 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min. Equivalently, 1500/20 = 75 beats/min.
questions.distractor_note: Heart rate depends on the R-R interval; the standard 25 mm/s conversion yields 1500 divided by small squares.

simulation.stem: Why does the sinoatrial (SA) node normally determine the heart rate?
options: It is the only cardiac site that can generate impulses without nerve stimulation.
It reaches the threshold for spontaneous discharge sooner than other pacemakers.
It conducts electrical impulses through ventricular muscle faster than Purkinje fibres.
Its cells have a more negative resting membrane potential than ventricular cells.
It receives stronger sympathetic input than any other pacemaker tissue.
simulation.explanation: The SA node has the highest normal intrinsic pacemaker rate. Its impulses reach subsidiary pacemakers before those slower sites discharge.
simulation.distractor_note: Blood supply, contraction strength and ventricular conduction speed do not set the normal pacemaker hierarchy. Other conducting tissues also show automaticity.

simulation.stem: Left ventricular pressure has risen to 45 mmHg. Left atrial pressure is 10 mmHg and aortic pressure is 85 mmHg. Which phase is most likely?
options: Rapid ventricular filling
Reduced ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric relaxation
Rapid ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric contraction
simulation.explanation: The mitral valve is closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure. The aortic valve remains closed because ventricular pressure is still below aortic pressure. Rising pressure with both valves closed indicates isovolumetric contraction.
simulation.distractor_note: Ejection requires ventricular pressure above aortic pressure, while filling requires ventricular pressure below left atrial pressure.

simulation.chapter: CVS-02 / Pressure tracing and ejection onset
simulation.stem: The diagram shows left ventricular pressure (solid) and aortic pressure (dashed). At which labelled point does aortic valve opening begin?
options: Point B
Point A
Point C
Point D
Point E
simulation.explanation: The aortic valve opens as rising left ventricular pressure first exceeds aortic pressure. On the plotted curves this happens at B. Point A precedes the pressure crossover; C and D occur later in ejection, and E follows valve closure.
simulation.distractor_note: All other labels are placed before or after the initial ventricular-aortic pressure crossover.

simulation.chapter: CVS-02 / Stroke volume and ejection fraction
simulation.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 140 mL and an end-systolic volume of 56 mL. What is its ejection fraction?
simulation.explanation: Stroke volume = 140 - 56 = 84 mL. Ejection fraction = (84/140) x 100 = 60%.
simulation.distractor_note: 84 mL is the stroke volume, not a percentage; 40% is the fraction remaining after systole.

simulation.stem: In complete AV dissociation, an atrium sometimes contracts while the tricuspid valve is closed. Which jugular venous finding may appear?
options: A persistently absent a wave
Intermittent giant v waves caused by atrial systole
Loss of the y descent with every normal beat
A regular arterial-type pulse in the jugular vein
Intermittent giant a waves
simulation.explanation: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve causes a sudden large rise in right atrial pressure, producing cannon or giant a waves.
simulation.distractor_note: The a wave reflects atrial contraction; the v wave mainly reflects atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed.

simulation.stem: Why does inspiration normally widen the split between the aortic and pulmonary components of the second heart sound?
options: Increased right ventricular filling delays mitral valve opening.
Increased right ventricular filling delays pulmonary valve closure.
Reduced right ventricular filling delays aortic valve closure.
Increased left ventricular filling delays tricuspid valve closure.
Reduced left ventricular filling delays the first heart sound.
simulation.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, often prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying P2 relative to A2.
simulation.distractor_note: S2 reflects semilunar valve closure, not AV valve opening or closure.

simulation.stem: A patient has backward blood flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole. Which valve disorder best explains this?
options: Mitral stenosis
Aortic stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation
simulation.explanation: Mitral regurgitation occurs when the mitral valve fails to prevent systolic backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
simulation.distractor_note: Mitral stenosis obstructs diastolic forward flow; aortic disorders affect flow across the aortic valve, and tricuspid regurgitation affects the right heart.

simulation.stem: Venous return rises while heart rate, afterload and contractility remain unchanged. What immediate change is expected in a normal ventricle?
options: A rise in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A fall in end-diastolic volume and stroke volume
A rise in stroke volume with a fall in end-diastolic volume
A fall in stroke volume despite a rise in end-diastolic volume
No change in stroke volume despite greater ventricular filling
simulation.explanation: More venous return increases ventricular filling and stretches cardiac fibres. On the ascending Frank-Starling relationship this raises force and stroke volume.
simulation.distractor_note: The Frank-Starling response links greater preload to greater output within physiological limits.

simulation.stem: Aortic pressure suddenly rises. For the first affected beat, ventricular filling and contractility are unchanged. What is the likely effect on stroke volume?
options: Stroke volume increases because aortic recoil becomes stronger.
Stroke volume increases because ventricular filling has increased.
Stroke volume stays constant because heart rate has not changed.
Stroke volume decreases because the ventricle ejects against greater pressure.
Stroke volume increases because the AV node conducts more quickly.
simulation.explanation: Greater afterload makes ventricular ejection more difficult. Before compensatory adjustments, end-systolic volume tends to increase and stroke volume decreases.
simulation.distractor_note: Aortic recoil, filling and AV conduction are not the mechanisms determining the first-beat afterload response.

simulation.chapter: CVS-05 / Contractility and ventricular function curve
simulation.stem: Two ventricular function curves are shown. At the same end-diastolic volume, curve X produces a larger stroke volume than curve Y. What best explains the difference?
options: Ventricular preload must be greater on curve X.
The heart rate must be lower on curve X.
The aortic valve must be closed throughout ejection on curve X.
The ventricular muscle must be less responsive to calcium on curve X.
Ventricular contractility is greater on curve X.
simulation.explanation: An upward shift of the Frank-Starling curve indicates greater stroke volume at the same preload, consistent with increased contractility.
simulation.distractor_note: The comparison holds end-diastolic volume constant, so increased preload is not the explanation; reduced calcium response would tend to reduce contractility.

simulation.stem: Oxygen consumption is 280 mL/min. Arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous oxygen content is 130 mL/L. What is cardiac output?
options: 4 L/min
2 L/min
3 L/min
5 L/min
7 L/min
simulation.explanation: Arterial-mixed venous oxygen content difference = 200 - 130 = 70 mL/L. Cardiac output = 280 mL/min divided by 70 mL/L = 4 L/min.
simulation.distractor_note: The Fick method divides oxygen consumption by the oxygen content difference, not by either concentration alone.

simulation.chapter: CVS-06 / Pressure work and oxygen demand
simulation.stem: At the same stroke volume and heart rate, which change generally increases myocardial oxygen demand more?
options: Pumping against a lower arterial pressure
Reducing the pressure needed to open the aortic valve
Pumping against a much higher arterial pressure
Lowering wall tension during ventricular ejection
Reducing the pressure difference across the aortic valve
simulation.explanation: Pressure work, which increases with afterload and myocardial wall tension, carries a high oxygen cost. Pumping the same volume against greater arterial pressure is more demanding.
simulation.distractor_note: The alternative changes reduce pressure load rather than increase it.

simulation.stem: According to Poiseuille's law, if a vessel radius is reduced to half while other factors remain constant, how does resistance change?
options: It becomes 2 times greater.
It becomes 4 times greater.
It becomes 16 times greater.
It becomes 8 times greater.
It becomes 16 times smaller.
simulation.explanation: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius. Halving radius therefore increases resistance by 2^4 = 16 times.
simulation.distractor_note: The fourth-power dependence is stronger than a linear, square or cubic change.

simulation.chapter: CVS-07 / Flow velocity and cross-sectional area
simulation.stem: Why is average blood-flow velocity normally much lower in capillaries than in the aorta?
options: The total capillary cross-sectional area is smaller than that of the aorta.
Capillaries receive a smaller total blood flow than the aorta in steady state.
Capillary pressure is lower, so red cells are stationary between heartbeats.
The combined cross-sectional area of all capillaries is much larger.
Blood viscosity is so much higher in capillaries that flow velocity must be zero.
simulation.explanation: For a given volume flow rate, average velocity equals flow divided by cross-sectional area. The enormous total capillary area produces low average velocity.
simulation.distractor_note: Flow continues in capillaries; the key comparison is total cross-sectional area, not the diameter of one capillary.

simulation.stem: Which isolated change increases the tendency for turbulent flow in a blood vessel?
options: An increase in blood viscosity
A decrease in blood density
An increase in blood-flow velocity
A decrease in vessel diameter
A decrease in the Reynolds number
simulation.explanation: Reynolds number increases with velocity, density and diameter, and decreases with viscosity. Increased velocity therefore makes turbulence more likely.
simulation.distractor_note: Higher viscosity and smaller diameter generally lower Reynolds number when other variables are held constant.

simulation.stem: A resting adult has a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg. Using the usual resting approximation, what is mean arterial pressure?
options: 75 mmHg
90 mmHg
85 mmHg
95 mmHg
105 mmHg
simulation.explanation: Pulse pressure = 120 - 75 = 45 mmHg. MAP is approximately diastolic pressure + one-third of pulse pressure = 75 + 15 = 90 mmHg.
simulation.distractor_note: MAP is not the simple arithmetic midpoint; diastole usually occupies more time at rest.

simulation.stem: In a healthy adult, cuff pressure is slowly released during blood-pressure measurement. Disappearance of Korotkoff sounds usually marks which pressure?
options: Systolic arterial pressure
Mean arterial pressure
Diastolic arterial pressure
Pulse pressure
Central venous pressure
simulation.explanation: As cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the brachial artery is open throughout the cardiac cycle and the characteristic Korotkoff sounds generally disappear.
simulation.distractor_note: The first appearance of sound usually marks systolic rather than diastolic pressure.

simulation.stem: A deep vein in one leg becomes obstructed, increasing pressure in vessels upstream. What local change most directly favours swelling?
options: An increase in plasma albumin concentration
A decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure
An increase in lymphatic drainage capacity
A decrease in capillary wall permeability
An increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure
simulation.explanation: Impaired venous drainage raises capillary pressure and promotes movement of fluid from capillaries into interstitial tissue.
simulation.distractor_note: Higher plasma oncotic pressure or stronger lymphatic removal would oppose fluid accumulation.

simulation.stem: A patient develops chronic swelling of an arm after axillary lymph nodes are removed. What is the main reason?
options: Arterial blood supply to the arm has completely stopped.
Red blood cells begin moving freely out of intact capillaries.
The heart pumps excess blood only into the affected arm.
Interstitial fluid and proteins cannot drain normally through lymph vessels.
Plasma albumin production increases sharply in the affected tissue.
simulation.explanation: Damage to lymphatic pathways reduces the return of interstitial fluid and proteins to the blood, producing lymphoedema.
simulation.distractor_note: Lymphoedema is caused by impaired lymph removal, not complete loss of arterial flow.

simulation.stem: Why does walking help return blood from the leg veins to the heart?
options: Muscle contractions compress veins while valves limit backward flow.
Venous valves in the calf actively push blood toward the heart.
Walking lowers all leg capillary pressures to zero.
Muscle compression pushes venous blood toward the feet through open valves.
Veins become less compliant and no longer experience gravity.
simulation.explanation: Contraction of leg muscles compresses nearby veins. One-way venous valves direct the displaced blood centrally, limiting pooling.
simulation.distractor_note: Venous valves are passive one-way structures; muscle compression supplies the pumping action.

simulation.stem: During exercise, working skeletal muscle produces more CO2, H+ and other metabolites. What local vascular response is expected?
options: Arteriolar constriction that reduces supply to active muscle
Arteriolar dilation that increases blood supply to the active muscle
Closure of all capillaries until the exercise finishes
A reduction in local flow despite increased oxygen demand
Selective closure of venous valves inside the muscle
simulation.explanation: Local metabolic vasodilators help match perfusion to greater tissue metabolic activity. Dilation reduces resistance and permits more flow.
simulation.distractor_note: Active tissue usually needs greater, not lower, local perfusion.

simulation.stem: Blood flow through a forearm artery is briefly blocked and then restored. Why may flow temporarily rise above its resting level?
options: Vasodilator metabolites built up while the tissue was underperfused.
The heart has permanently increased the forearm's blood supply.
The arterial pulse wave has stopped travelling through the arm.
The blockage permanently removed vascular resistance.
Venous valves now actively force arterial blood toward the hand.
simulation.explanation: During the occlusion, tissue oxygen delivery falls and local vasodilatory signals build up. When flow resumes, dilated resistance vessels produce transient reactive hyperaemia.
simulation.distractor_note: Reactive hyperaemia is a temporary local response to preceding flow interruption.

simulation.stem: The graph shows blood flow across a range of perfusion pressures. Between points B and C, why is flow nearly constant despite rising pressure?
options: Arteriolar resistance falls as perfusion pressure rises.
Cardiac output stops changing throughout the entire body.
Arteriolar resistance rises as perfusion pressure rises.
Venous blood begins flowing backward into the artery.
The tissue stops consuming oxygen over this pressure range.
simulation.explanation: For approximately constant flow Q, a higher perfusion pressure requires a higher local resistance (Q = pressure difference / resistance). The plateau reflects autoregulatory adjustment.
simulation.distractor_note: Falling resistance alongside increasing pressure would increase, rather than stabilize, flow.

simulation.chapter: CVS-11 / Baroreceptor reflex fall in BP
simulation.stem: A person suddenly loses blood and arterial pressure falls. Which immediate autonomic change helps restore pressure?
options: Reduced sympathetic activity and increased vagal activity
Reduced sympathetic and reduced vagal activity together
Increased sympathetic activity and reduced vagal activity
Increased vagal activity with arteriolar dilation
No change in autonomic outflow until blood volume recovers
simulation.explanation: Less stretch of carotid and aortic baroreceptors reduces afferent firing. The medulla responds with increased sympathetic and reduced parasympathetic outflow.
simulation.distractor_note: Increased vagal activity would tend to slow the heart rather than compensate for falling pressure.

simulation.stem: A patient develops rapidly rising intracranial pressure with impaired brainstem perfusion. Which combination is typical of the Cushing response?
options: Increased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Decreased arterial pressure with reflex slowing of the heart
Increased arterial pressure with sustained reflex tachycardia
Decreased arterial pressure with complete loss of sympathetic tone
Unchanged arterial pressure with marked peripheral vasodilation
simulation.explanation: Reduced medullary perfusion causes a powerful sympathetic rise in systemic pressure. The resulting arterial hypertension stimulates baroreceptors, producing reflex bradycardia.
simulation.distractor_note: The raised pressure is a compensatory response to brainstem ischemia; bradycardia is secondary to the baroreflex.

simulation.stem: Rapid infusion of fluid increases venous return and stretches the right atrium. Which reflex response may help accommodate the larger venous return?
options: Heart rate may decrease because atrial stretch directly increases vagal outflow.
Heart rate may increase as atrial stretch activates a reflex.
Heart rate may remain unchanged because atrial stretch has no reflex effects.
Heart rate may decrease because venous return is reduced by the fluid infusion.
Heart rate may increase only if the arterial baroreceptors first detect hypotension.
simulation.explanation: The atrial stretch (Bainbridge) reflex can increase heart rate when venous return and atrial filling rise. It is distinct from the arterial baroreceptor response to elevated blood pressure.
simulation.distractor_note: Atrial distension can elicit reflex tachycardia without requiring arterial hypotension. The infusion increases rather than reduces venous return.

simulation.stem: Immediately after a person stands up quickly, before reflex compensation has fully developed, what tends to happen?
options: Venous pooling decreases and ventricular filling rises.
Venous pooling increases and venous return to the heart falls.
Venous pressure in the feet falls below pressure at heart level.
Cardiac output rises because gravity pushes blood toward the chest.
Cerebral blood flow increases because the head is now above the heart.
simulation.explanation: Gravity increases hydrostatic pressure and pooling in dependent veins. This reduces central venous return, initially lowering stroke volume and potentially cerebral perfusion.
simulation.distractor_note: Without compensation, standing does not drive leg blood centrally or raise head-level perfusion.

simulation.stem: A person loses a substantial amount of blood. What sequence most directly explains the initial fall in cardiac output?
options: Lower blood volume directly raises ventricular end-diastolic volume.
Lower blood volume immediately increases plasma oncotic pressure enough to raise output.
Lower blood volume causes the aortic valve to open earlier at a higher stroke volume.
Lower blood volume leads to lower venous return and ventricular filling.
Lower blood volume raises pulmonary venous return above systemic venous return.
simulation.explanation: Blood loss reduces circulating volume and venous return, which reduces preload and stroke volume. Reflex vasoconstriction may defend pressure but cannot automatically restore lost flow.
simulation.distractor_note: Loss of circulating volume does not directly raise preload or stroke volume.

simulation.stem: A patient with severe infection has widespread arteriolar dilation and low arterial pressure. Which shock mechanism is most likely?
options: Hypovolaemic shock caused mainly by external blood loss
Cardiogenic shock caused mainly by poor ventricular pumping
Obstructive shock caused mainly by mechanical blockage of blood flow
A normal circulation with a temporary rise in vascular resistance
Distributive shock caused mainly by reduced systemic vascular resistance
simulation.explanation: Sepsis can produce profound vasodilation and loss of vascular tone, lowering total peripheral resistance and effective perfusion pressure. This is distributive shock.
simulation.distractor_note: The defining event in this stem is widespread low resistance rather than haemorrhage, pump failure or obstruction.

simulation.stem: A patient with left ventricular failure develops breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. What pressure change most directly promotes fluid movement into the lungs?
options: Increased pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure
Decreased pulmonary venous pressure
Increased plasma oncotic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Decreased hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries
Increased lymphatic drainage with unchanged capillary pressure
simulation.explanation: Poor left ventricular output raises pressure upstream in the left atrium and pulmonary veins. Higher pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes filtration and pulmonary oedema.
simulation.distractor_note: Fluid filtration increases with raised hydrostatic pressure; higher oncotic pressure would tend to oppose it.

simulation.stem: An obstruction mainly affects blood supply to the lateral surface of a cerebral hemisphere. Which major cerebral artery is most likely involved?
options: Anterior cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Anterior communicating artery
Middle cerebral artery
Basilar artery
simulation.explanation: The middle cerebral artery supplies much of the lateral cerebral hemisphere. The anterior cerebral artery supplies much of the medial frontal and parietal surface.
simulation.distractor_note: The anterior and posterior cerebral arteries supply other major territories; communicating arteries are chiefly connectors in the arterial circle.

simulation.stem: The cerebral aqueduct becomes blocked while CSF production continues. Which ventricles are expected to enlarge first?
options: The fourth ventricle alone
The third and fourth ventricles only
The lateral ventricles and fourth ventricle only
The lateral and third ventricles
The fourth ventricle and central canal only
simulation.explanation: The aqueduct links the third to the fourth ventricle. Obstruction causes CSF to accumulate upstream in the third and lateral ventricles.
simulation.distractor_note: The fourth ventricle lies downstream of the aqueduct and is not the primary site of enlargement in an isolated aqueduct blockage.

simulation.stem: Mean arterial pressure is 95 mmHg and intracranial pressure is 15 mmHg. Assuming cerebral venous pressure is not higher than intracranial pressure, what is cerebral perfusion pressure?
options: 65 mmHg
75 mmHg
80 mmHg
95 mmHg
110 mmHg
simulation.explanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is approximately MAP - ICP when ICP is the effective downstream pressure: 95 - 15 = 80 mmHg.
simulation.distractor_note: Perfusion pressure is a difference between driving and downstream pressures; it is not the MAP alone.

simulation.stem: Why does most left ventricular coronary blood flow occur during diastole rather than systole?
options: The left coronary artery is closed by the aortic valve during systole.
Blood in coronary arteries contains oxygen only during diastole.
The heart stops using oxygen during systole.
Pulmonary venous pressure becomes higher than aortic pressure during systole.
Contracting left ventricular muscle compresses vessels within its wall.
simulation.explanation: During left ventricular systole, high intramyocardial pressure compresses coronary vessels, especially in the subendocardium. Relaxation during diastole permits better perfusion.
simulation.distractor_note: Coronary arterial openings remain connected to the aorta; the critical factor is compression by contracting myocardium.

simulation.stem: One group of alveoli is poorly ventilated while nearby alveoli are well ventilated. What happens to the small pulmonary arteries supplying the poorly ventilated region?
options: They dilate, directing more blood toward the poorly ventilated alveoli.
They remain unchanged because oxygen never affects pulmonary resistance.
They constrict only if systemic arterial pressure is also high.
They close because all pulmonary arteries normally lack smooth muscle.
They constrict, directing more blood toward better-ventilated alveoli.
simulation.explanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary arteriolar constriction. This helps divert flow toward alveoli where oxygen uptake is more effective.
simulation.distractor_note: The pulmonary hypoxic response is opposite to the usual local hypoxic vasodilation in systemic tissues.

simulation.stem: During exercise, pulmonary blood flow increases greatly but pulmonary arterial pressure rises relatively little. What helps explain this?
options: Most pulmonary capillaries close as flow increases.
Previously underperfused capillaries open and existing vessels widen.
Pulmonary vascular resistance increases in direct proportion to flow.
The right ventricle stops pumping blood during exercise.
The alveoli stop exchanging gases while blood flow rises.
simulation.explanation: Recruitment of additional pulmonary capillaries and distension of vessels increase the total flow capacity, limiting the rise in pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure.
simulation.distractor_note: Recruitment and distension expand, not reduce, pulmonary vascular capacity.

simulation.stem: After firm stroking of the skin, redness spreads beyond the directly stimulated line. What produces this surrounding flare?
options: An axon reflex causing nearby arterioles to dilate
Clotting of capillaries at the site of injury
A sudden fall in total circulating blood volume
Closure of all precapillary sphincters around the area
Direct filtration of red blood cells into the epidermis
simulation.explanation: The flare of the triple response is produced by an antidromic axon reflex that dilates vessels around the stimulated region.
simulation.distractor_note: The wheal reflects increased local permeability, whereas the flare is spreading arteriolar vasodilation.

simulation.stem: What change occurs in the pulmonary circulation with the newborn's first breaths?
options: Pulmonary vascular resistance rises as alveolar oxygen rises.
Pulmonary blood flow stops because placental blood flow has ended.
Pulmonary vascular resistance falls as the lungs expand and oxygen rises.
The ductus venosus begins carrying blood from the right ventricle.
Systemic vascular resistance falls because the placenta remains connected.
simulation.explanation: Lung expansion and increased alveolar oxygen reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, raising pulmonary blood flow. Loss of the placenta simultaneously tends to raise systemic vascular resistance.
simulation.distractor_note: The first breaths promote pulmonary vasodilation, not vasoconstriction.

simulation.stem: Which pair of electrodes forms standard bipolar lead I in an ECG?
options: Right arm (negative) and left leg (positive)
Left arm (negative) and left leg (positive)
Left leg (negative) and right arm (positive)
Right arm (negative) and left arm (positive)
Left arm (negative) and right arm (positive)
simulation.explanation: Standard lead I measures the potential difference LA(+) minus RA(-). Lead II uses RA(-) and LL(+), while lead III uses LA(-) and LL(+).
simulation.distractor_note: Lead II and III use the left-leg electrode; reversing the lead I polarity is also incorrect.

simulation.stem: In the ECG strip, the distance between consecutive R waves is 20 small squares. The paper speed is 25 mm/s. What is the heart rate?
options: 60 beats/min
75 beats/min
80 beats/min
100 beats/min
120 beats/min
simulation.explanation: At 25 mm/s, one small square = 0.04 s. Twenty squares = 0.8 s per beat, giving 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min. Equivalently, 1500/20 = 75 beats/min.
simulation.distractor_note: Heart rate depends on the R-R interval; the standard 25 mm/s conversion yields 1500 divided by small squares.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.stem: A severe rise in intracranial pressure produces systemic hypertension with reflex bradycardia. What is this response?
options: Lung hypoxia reflex.
Atrial stretch reflex.
Bainbridge reflex.
Cushing reflex.
questions.explanation: The Cushing response reflects brainstem ischaemia driving systemic hypertension, with baroreflex-mediated bradycardia. Brain perfusion is threatened as raised intracranial pressure compresses cerebral vessels.
distractors: Pulmonary hypoxic vasoconstriction is a local lung response.
Atrial stretch does not explain raised ICP-driven hypertension.
Bainbridge responds to increased atrial filling.

questions.stem: Which pressure relationship helps prevent fluid accumulation in normal pulmonary alveoli?
options: Pulmonary capillary pressure consistently exceeds systemic arterial pressure.
Absence of plasma proteins in pulmonary capillaries.
Relatively low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.
Higher alveolar protein pressure than in capillary plasma.
questions.explanation: Low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure relative to plasma oncotic forces helps minimise filtration into air spaces.
distractors: Pulmonary capillary pressure is much lower than systemic arterial pressure.
Plasma proteins contribute the inward oncotic force.
Alveolar spaces normally contain little free fluid and protein.

questions.chapter: Chapter 26 — Cutaneous Circulation and the Triple Response
questions.section: 2. Skin blood flow in shock
questions.stem: A patient in compensated haemorrhagic shock has cold, pale skin. Which mechanism accounts for this?
options: Increased sympathetic cutaneous vasoconstriction.
Loss of vasomotor drive causing widespread dilation.
Increased skin capillary blood volume from vasodilation.
Direct activation of warm-sensitive skin receptors.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic constriction reduces skin flow to preserve perfusion for vital organs, producing pallor and coolness.
distractors: Loss of sympathetic tone would usually warm and flush skin.
Higher cutaneous blood volume tends to increase redness.
The primary response is systemic compensation, not skin warming.

questions.stem: A cuff that is far too small is used on a large upper arm. Which measurement error is likely?
options: No systematic effect on cuff pressure.
An undersized cuff gives a falsely high reading.
Only diastolic pressure becomes unmeasurable.
Falsely low BP from excessive arterial unloading.
questions.explanation: An undersized cuff transmits pressure poorly around a large arm and commonly overestimates measured pressure.
distractors: Cuff size materially affects readings.
Both systolic and diastolic measurements may be distorted.
A small cuff usually overestimates rather than underestimates BP.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.stem: The CSF volume is about 150 mL and production is 550 mL/day. Approximately how many complete turnovers occur per day?
options: About 4.
About 2.
About 1.
About 6.
questions.explanation: Dividing daily production by total CSF volume gives 550/150 ≈ 3.7 turnovers each day.
distractors: Two turnovers would require about 300 mL/day.
One turnover would represent only about 150 mL/day.
Six turnovers would correspond to around 900 mL/day.

questions.section: 8. Basic rhythm assessment (supplementary)
questions.stem: Which recording satisfies the basic chapter criteria for a normal sinus rhythm at rest?
options: Rate 72/min, equal R–R gaps, identical preceding P waves, PR 0.16 s.
Rate 72/min, equal R–R gaps, no visible P waves, PR not measurable.
Rate 72/min, unequal R–R gaps, identical preceding P waves, PR 0.16 s.
Rate 72/min, equal R–R gaps, identical preceding P waves, PR 0.26 s.
questions.explanation: Normal sinus rhythm at rest requires an appropriate rate, regular R–R intervals, a consistent P before each QRS, and normal conduction intervals; the listed 0.16-s PR satisfies this.
distractors: Without a visible P wave before each QRS, sinus origin is not established.
Unequal R–R intervals do not satisfy the chapter’s basic regularity criterion.
A PR of 0.26 s exceeds the chapter’s stated 0.12–0.20-s range.

questions.stem: Increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure while other Starling forces stay unchanged tends to produce what?
options: Decreased outward fluid filtration.
More fluid filtration into tissues.
Reversal of lymphatic flow.
Increased plasma oncotic attraction.
questions.explanation: A higher capillary hydrostatic force favours filtration across the microvascular wall toward tissue. Raising venous pressure is one way to produce this hydrostatic change.
distractors: The pressure favours outward, not reduced, filtration.
Lymphatic flow generally responds to excess tissue fluid rather than reversing.
Plasma oncotic pressure does not automatically increase.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.stem: A patient develops cardiac tamponade. Why can stroke volume fall despite a normal blood volume?
options: Tamponade increases functional ventricular compliance.
Tamponade directly raises venous return above normal.
The aortic valve cannot open due solely to a high heart rate.
High pericardial pressure restricts ventricular filling.
questions.explanation: Elevated intrapericardial pressure limits end-diastolic filling and preload, reducing stroke volume. The restricted ventricular volume prevents an adequate Frank–Starling response.
distractors: Tamponade reduces the ability of ventricles to expand.
Venous return and effective filling become impaired.
Valvular opening depends on pressure, but reduced preload is the central problem.

questions.section: 7. What happens to veins in the head when standing?
questions.stem: Why are superficial neck veins often less distended in a healthy person who stands upright?
options: Venous pressure decreases above the heart.
The venae cavae reverse their direction of blood flow.
Systemic venous pressure exceeds aortic systolic pressure.
The skull's arteries pull venous valves fully open.
questions.explanation: Gravity lowers venous pressure above the heart; collapsible superficial veins can flatten at low transmural pressure.
distractors: Venous return does not normally reverse direction.
Systemic venous pressure remains far below aortic systolic pressure.
Arterial flow does not open venous valves in the neck.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: Arterial pressure inside an arteriole is unchanged, but pressure in its surrounding tissue rises. What happens to transmural pressure?
options: It decreases because the pressure difference narrows.
It increases because the pressure difference widens.
It becomes identical to intravascular arterial pressure.
It remains fixed because arterial pressure is unchanged.
