questions.explanation: Transmural pressure equals internal pressure minus surrounding tissue pressure; increasing the latter reduces the difference.
distractors: A higher external pressure reduces, rather than widens, the difference.
It equals internal pressure only when external pressure is zero.
Transmural pressure depends on both internal and external pressure.

questions.stem: A severely underperfused patient begins breathing rapidly, although the lungs were initially healthy. What drives this change?
options: Increased aerobic ATP production stimulates breathing.
Suppression of the peripheral chemoreceptors stimulates breathing.
Lactic acidosis stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.
High tissue oxygen content increases respiratory drive.
questions.explanation: Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery promotes anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. The resulting acidemia can stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors and increase ventilation; reduced oxygen delivery alone is not equivalent to low arterial oxygen tension.
distractors: Aerobic metabolism is limited by inadequate oxygen delivery.
Chemoreceptor stimulation, rather than suppression, promotes respiration.
Excess oxygen is not the initiating problem in shock.

questions.section: 5. Why can low plasma proteins cause oedema?
questions.stem: Why may advanced liver disease cause generalised oedema even without venous obstruction?
options: Excess albumin synthesis draws water into tissues.
Less albumin synthesis reduces plasma oncotic pressure.
A rise in plasma protein concentration stops absorption.
Liver failure directly shuts every lymphatic valve.
questions.explanation: Reduced albumin production lowers intravascular colloid oncotic pressure, allowing more net filtration and oedema.
distractors: Advanced liver disease commonly reduces albumin synthesis.
Plasma protein concentration is decreased, not increased.
Lymphatic valve closure is not the universal mechanism.

questions.stem: How does local hypoxia affect most systemic arterioles versus pulmonary arterioles?
options: Systemic vessels constrict while pulmonary vessels dilate.
Both primarily constrict to lower oxygen delivery.
Both remain relatively insensitive to tissue oxygen.
Systemic vessels dilate; pulmonary vessels constrict.
questions.explanation: Systemic hypoxic tissues commonly dilate to improve supply, whereas low alveolar oxygen constricts adjacent pulmonary arterioles to improve ventilation–perfusion matching.
distractors: The response directions have been reversed.
Systemic tissues usually need increased flow in hypoxia.
Oxygen tension influences both beds, but their dominant local responses differ.

questions.stem: A pressure tracing shows atrial contraction shortly after an ECG P wave and ventricular contraction shortly after QRS. What principle explains both delays?
options: Electrical excitation normally precedes the mechanical response of cardiac muscle.
Mechanical contraction normally finishes before electrical activation begins in the chamber.
The T wave must occur before either chamber can begin contraction.
Atrial and ventricular pressures directly create the corresponding ECG waves.
questions.explanation: The electrical depolarisation that activates cardiac muscle precedes its force development. P precedes atrial systole, and QRS precedes ventricular systole.
distractors: This reverses the normal electrical-to-mechanical sequence.
The T wave reflects ventricular electrical recovery, after ventricular depolarisation.
Pressure changes follow electrical activation and are not what skin ECG leads measure.

questions.section: 7. Other inputs, and the lecture’s “exceptions”
questions.stem: A student faints after receiving distressing news, with a slow pulse and low arterial pressure. Which mechanism best matches the lecture?
options: Severe medullary ischaemia causing a Cushing pressor response.
Emotional inhibition of pressor activity with vagal predominance.
Metabolic stimulation of the heart’s sympathetic beta-1 receptors.
Atrial volume-receptor firing after excessive fluid infusion.
questions.explanation: Fear or grief can favour a depressor, vagal response with bradycardia, vasodilation and hypotension.
distractors: Cushing physiology produces hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
β₁ stimulation would generally raise the pulse and contractility.
Overfilled atria may produce a faster pulse in the described reflex.

questions.stem: What extra perspective do the chest leads V1–V6 add to the standard limb-lead views?
options: They replace voltage measurement with intracardiac pressure.
They remove the need to record the frontal electrical plane.
They isolate atrial electrical activity from ventricular activity.
They show cardiac electrical vectors in the horizontal plane.
questions.explanation: The limb leads provide frontal-plane views, while the precordial leads examine the same heart from different points around the horizontal plane.
distractors: Chest leads, like limb leads, still record surface electrical potentials.
Frontal and horizontal views complement rather than replace one another.
Both sets of leads record combined cardiac electrical events.

questions.stem: During progressive shock, capillary hydrostatic pressure paradoxically rises while systemic arterial pressure is falling. Which microvascular pattern best explains it?
options: Precapillary constriction with freely draining venules.
Increased venular drainage with reduced capillary entry.
Open capillary entry with constricted venules.
Precapillary constriction with widened venous outlets.
questions.explanation: With capillary entry relatively open but venular outflow restricted, blood stagnates and local capillary pressure rises, driving fluid into the interstitium.
distractors: Lower entry with free outflow would not cause the described stasis.
Greater drainage would reduce rather than increase local stagnation.
Both reduced entry and improved drainage favour lower capillary pressure.

questions.section: 2. Systolic and diastolic failure: can't squeeze, or can't fill?
questions.stem: A stiff ventricle has high filling pressure but a preserved ejection fraction. What is the primary defect?
options: Impaired relaxation and filling.
Increased contractility and ejection.
Reduced electrical activation of the SA node.
Excessive ventricular compliance.
questions.explanation: Diastolic failure reflects impaired relaxation and stiff ventricular filling; the fraction of blood ejected can remain normal despite elevated filling pressures and reduced filling volume.
distractors: Increased contractility is not the primary defect.
SA-node dysfunction does not define diastolic heart failure.
A stiff ventricle has reduced, not excessive, compliance.

questions.stem: Lead II has an upright QRS while aVR has a downward QRS during the same beat. What best explains the difference?
options: Each lead projects the same electrical vector onto a different axis.
One lead measures depolarisation and the other repolarisation.
The two leads record different mechanical contractions.
Atrial and ventricular activity alternate between the leads on each beat.
questions.explanation: A lead is a directional electrical view. The normal mean ventricular depolarisation vector points generally towards Lead II and away from aVR.
distractors: Both QRS complexes represent ventricular depolarisation, despite opposite polarity.
Both leads sample the electrical activity of the same heartbeat.
Lead orientation does not change the sequence of atrial and ventricular activation.

questions.stem: A patient with marked polycythaemia has elevated haematocrit. What is the expected direct effect on systemic flow resistance?
options: Lower viscosity and lower total vascular resistance.
Higher viscosity and lower resistance.
Higher viscosity and higher resistance.
Lower viscosity and higher resistance.
questions.explanation: More red cells increase blood viscosity and consequently vascular resistance, raising the heart's workload.
distractors: Both properties generally increase, not decrease.
Higher viscosity raises resistance rather than lowering it.
Lower viscosity does not follow from higher haematocrit.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 1. Why the brain can't wait for blood
questions.stem: Why can a brief complete interruption of cerebral blood flow cause unconsciousness within seconds?
options: The brain has very limited stores of oxygen and fuel.
The brain stores enough ATP for several minutes of activity.
The cerebral circulation can switch immediately to venous oxygen.
The brainstem normally stops all electrical activity first.
questions.explanation: Neural activity depends on continuous perfusion because energy and oxygen reserves are small; the lecture cites roughly 10 seconds.
distractors: Adequate stored energy does not sustain function for many minutes.
Venous blood cannot replace arterial oxygen delivery.
The lecture describes cortical vulnerability, with brainstem structures relatively more resistant.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: A resting muscle suddenly becomes active while systemic arterial pressure stays steady. What most directly increases its blood supply?
options: Its large veins reduce their compliance.
Its arteries increase their driving pressure.
Its local arterioles reduce their resistance.
Its local capillaries develop stronger contractions.
questions.explanation: Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. With arterial pressure unchanged, the only way to get more flow is lower resistance, and the resistance that tissues control is in their arterioles. Metabolites from the working muscle relax those arterioles.
distractors: Vein compliance mainly affects stored volume, not the main resistance to flow.
The stem states that systemic arterial pressure remains steady.
Capillaries lack the smooth muscle needed for this response.

questions.stem: At one instant, Lead I records +0.4 mV and Lead III records −0.2 mV. What must Lead II record?
options: −0.2 mV, from using the third lead alone.
+0.6 mV, from adding their magnitudes.
+0.2 mV, from adding the signed voltages.
−0.6 mV, from subtracting the two values.
questions.explanation: Einthoven’s law is V(II) = V(I) + V(III). Therefore +0.4 + (−0.2) = +0.2 mV at the same instant.
distractors: Lead II is obtained by combining the two measured limb-lead voltages.
The negative sign of Lead III must be retained in the sum.
This reverses the sign of the result rather than adding the signed voltages.

questions.section: 10. Why can veins hold more blood than arteries?
questions.stem: Compared with a large artery, why can a large vein store more blood for a small rise in pressure?
options: Venous walls contain more elastic recoil tissue than aorta.
Veins have high compliance and distensible walls.
Venous vessels are made mostly of cardiac muscle.
Venous pressure generally exceeds aortic systolic pressure.
questions.explanation: Veins have thin distensible walls and high compliance, so volume changes greatly for modest pressure changes.
distractors: Large arteries have substantial elastic tissue; veins serve mainly as capacitance vessels.
Veins are not cardiac muscle.
Systemic venous pressure is much lower than aortic systolic pressure; compliance concerns volume change per unit pressure change.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: A region of heart muscle starts working harder. Which local product of its own metabolism helps increase its blood flow?
options: Serotonin released by nearby platelets.
Angiotensin II formed in the blood.
Noradrenaline from sympathetic nerves.
Adenosine formed as ATP is used up.
questions.explanation: Working muscle uses ATP faster, and its breakdown products (adenosine, ADP, AMP) build up and dilate the local arterioles. Flow rises in proportion to how hard the tissue works, which is why the heart relies so heavily on this.
distractors: Platelet serotonin constricts vessels, and it comes from platelets, not from the working muscle.
Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor, not a product of the muscle’s metabolism.
Noradrenaline is a nerve transmitter that mainly constricts arterioles via α₁ receptors.

questions.stem: What physiological purpose is served by slow conduction through the AV node?
options: It prevents the impulse from ever reaching the ventricular myocardium.
It ensures ventricles eject before the atria contract.
It allows the aortic valve to remain open during atrial systole.
It allows atrial contraction to finish ventricular filling.
questions.explanation: The AV delay separates atrial and ventricular activation so atrial systole can augment ventricular filling before ventricular systole.
distractors: Normal impulses subsequently travel through His and Purkinje fibres.
The sequence is atrial activation before ventricular activation.
The aortic valve remains closed during ordinary atrial systole.

questions.section: 5. Why can tachycardia cause ischaemia?
questions.stem: Why is a patient with significant coronary narrowing more vulnerable to angina when heart rate rises sharply?
options: The P wave disappears and blocks blood flow.
Myocardial oxygen consumption falls below baseline.
The coronary sinus develops arterial hypertension.
Shorter diastole and higher myocardial demand.
questions.explanation: Tachycardia increases cardiac oxygen demand and shortens diastole, reducing the time available for left ventricular coronary perfusion.
distractors: An absent P wave is not the explanation of demand-related angina.
Myocardial work and oxygen consumption generally rise with tachycardia.
The primary limitation is coronary supply through stenosed arteries during shortened diastole.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the updated interpretation of capillary fluid balance?
options: The glycocalyx regulates filtration; lymph returns excess fluid.
Lymphatic vessels play no role when hydrostatic pressure is normal.
Most capillaries continuously reabsorb nearly all filtered fluid at their venous ends.
Interstitial proteins do not affect exchange at any capillary.
questions.explanation: The revised Starling model includes the glycocalyx and emphasises that sustained net filtration is normally cleared by lymphatics.
distractors: Lymphatic return remains vital even at normal pressures.
The classical arterial filtration–venous reabsorption picture overstates sustained reabsorption.
Protein distributions can influence effective oncotic gradients.

questions.stem: Minutes after a severe allergic exposure, a patient's pressure drops with generalised swelling. Which vascular action is most relevant?
options: Histamine-related dilatation with increased capillary permeability.
Generalised constriction with reduced capillary permeability.
Increased myocardial pump function with reduced venous capacitance.
Selective haemorrhage into the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis releases mediators including histamine that widen vessels and increase capillary leakage, reducing effective perfusion.
distractors: Anaphylaxis typically causes dilation and increased leak.
Higher pump performance would not explain the sudden widespread leakage.
Occult bleeding is not the primary allergic vascular mechanism.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.section: 6. What raises or lowers end-diastolic volume?
questions.stem: After standing suddenly, a healthy person has a transient fall in end-diastolic volume. Which cause is most direct?
options: Increased atrial contraction generating excess preload.
Increased circulating red-cell mass.
Greater coronary artery blood flow.
Venous pooling reducing return to the heart.
questions.explanation: Gravity shifts blood into compliant leg veins, decreasing venous return and end-diastolic filling. Stroke volume then falls transiently by Frank–Starling physiology.
distractors: Atrial contraction tends to increase rather than reduce filling.
Red-cell mass does not change in seconds with posture.
Coronary flow does not explain the immediate preload decline.

questions.stem: How does normal inspiration tend to assist systemic venous return?
options: It increases right atrial pressure and reduces abdominal pressure.
It closes all systemic venous valves simultaneously.
It increases peripheral venous capacitance until return stops.
Lower chest pressure draws venous blood toward the heart.
questions.explanation: Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure and promotes a pressure gradient drawing blood from peripheral veins to the thorax.
distractors: Lower rather than higher thoracic pressure assists inflow.
Venous valves do not all close in inspiration.
Return is generally supported rather than abolished.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: An exercising leg receives increased blood flow while its muscle continues contracting. What is this response called?
options: Active hyperaemia driven by ongoing tissue metabolism.
Reactive hyperaemia following a temporary flow block.
Baroreflex vasodilation after systemic arterial pressure rises.
Autoregulation that holds its flow at rest level.
questions.explanation: Active hyperaemia is the rise in flow while a tissue is working: its metabolites dilate the arterioles for as long as activity continues. Reactive hyperaemia is the surge after a blockage is released.
distractors: Reactive hyperaemia is a surge after an obstruction ends.
The increase originates largely from local demand, not a pressure-rise baroreflex.
The flow rises above baseline rather than staying constant.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.section: 3. Two mechanisms: myogenic and metabolic
questions.stem: Two cylindrical vessels have equal transmural pressure, but vessel X has twice the radius of vessel Y. How do their required wall tensions compare?
options: Both vessels require exactly the same wall tension.
Vessel X requires half the wall tension of Y.
Vessel X requires four times the tension of Y.
Vessel X requires twice the wall tension of Y.
questions.explanation: For a cylinder, wall tension T = P × r. With equal transmural pressure, the vessel with twice the radius needs twice the tension. This is why a capillary’s tiny radius lets a one-cell wall withstand blood pressure.
distractors: Equal pressure alone does not make tension equal.
Half the tension would apply to half the radius.
A fourfold difference does not follow the linear radius relation.

questions.stem: Why does persistent lactic acidosis make circulatory shock harder to reverse?
options: It prevents further fluid filtration from capillaries.
It depresses contraction and catecholamine responses.
It directly restores aerobic ATP production.
It increases ventricular force and vascular responsiveness.
questions.explanation: Acidosis from anaerobic metabolism weakens cardiac pumping and reduces vascular response to catecholamines, undermining compensation.
distractors: Acidosis does not reliably prevent fluid movement into tissues.
Aerobic ATP generation still requires oxygen.
Acidosis impairs rather than strengthens these functions.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: Which of these locally released substances dilates arterioles?
options: Histamine
Endothelin-1
Serotonin
Angiotensin II
questions.explanation: Histamine, released from mast cells in injury and allergy, relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle (via H₂ receptors) and makes capillaries leakier, which is why inflamed tissue turns red and swollen.
distractors: Endothelin-1 from the endothelium is one of the most powerful constrictors known.
Serotonin from activated platelets constricts the injured vessel to limit bleeding.
Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and raises resistance.

questions.section: 3. What you see, and why
questions.stem: A previously anxious patient with severe prolonged shock becomes apathetic and poorly responsive. Which explanation is most concerning?
options: Red-cell production has rapidly restored oxygen delivery.
Skin vasoconstriction has resolved the shock.
The skeletal-muscle pump has become overactive.
Worsening cerebral ischaemia impairs brain function.
questions.explanation: Restlessness can accompany early sympathetic arousal; later apathy may indicate worsening cerebral ischaemia and failing perfusion.
distractors: Erythropoiesis cannot rapidly reverse acute circulatory collapse.
An improvement in perfusion would not account for deterioration.
The muscle pump does not explain progressive depressed consciousness.

questions.stem: An ECG machine runs at 25 mm/s. How much time passes while the paper advances by 1 mm horizontally?
questions.explanation: At a speed of 25 mm each second, 1 mm represents 1/25 s = 0.04 s, the duration of one small horizontal grid square.
distractors: 0.10 s does not correspond to a 1-mm horizontal square at this speed.
0.50 s would occupy 12.5 small squares.
0.20 s is the time represented by one 5-mm large square.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.stem: A cerebral vessel ruptures and blood enters brain tissue. Which type of cerebrovascular event is present?
options: Cerebral hypoglycaemia.
Embolic ischaemia.
Thrombotic ischaemia.
Haemorrhagic stroke.
questions.explanation: Haemorrhagic stroke results from rupture of a vessel, whereas ischaemic stroke results from interrupted arterial supply.
distractors: Hypoglycaemia causes global dysfunction rather than vessel rupture.
Embolism blocks flow rather than directly representing vessel rupture.
Thrombosis obstructs an artery instead of rupturing it.

questions.section: 4. Gravity, posture and the lung's blood reservoir
questions.stem: A person lies down after standing upright. What happens to pulmonary blood volume in the lecture's illustration?
options: It falls by approximately 400 mL.
It remains fixed regardless of posture.
It rises by approximately 400 mL.
It falls until alveolar flow stops.
questions.explanation: Supine positioning redistributes blood centrally, increasing the pulmonary blood reservoir by about 400 mL in the lecture.
distractors: The lecture describes an increase, not decrease, on lying down.
Pulmonary blood volume varies with posture.
Blood flow does not normally stop merely because someone lies down.

questions.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL and an end-systolic volume of 55 mL. What is its stroke volume?
options: 75 mL.
55 mL.
questions.explanation: Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV, so 130 − 55 = 75 mL per beat.
distractors: One hundred thirty mL is end-diastolic volume.
Fifty-five mL is end-systolic volume.
Adding EDV and ESV does not give stroke volume.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.stem: How does CSF substantially reduce the effective weight of the brain?
options: It increases the brain's intrinsic density.
It provides buoyant support against gravity.
It reduces blood volume to near zero.
It directly reduces the brain's oxygen consumption.
questions.explanation: Immersion provides buoyancy, reducing the brain's effective supported weight from roughly 1400–1500 g to around 50 g.
distractors: The tissue density does not increase to create buoyancy.
Brain blood volume remains substantial.
Lower oxygen consumption does not explain mechanical support.

questions.chapter: Chapter 8 — Measuring Cardiac Output and the Work of the Heart
questions.section: 3. Where do the oxygen measurements come from?
questions.stem: In a whole-body Fick measurement, which blood should the return-side oxygen sample represent?
options: Oxygenated blood in a systemic artery.
Mixed venous blood entering the lungs.
Blood in a single peripheral venule.
Capillary blood from active skeletal muscle only.
questions.explanation: A mixed venous sample from pulmonary artery reflects oxygen after extraction across the whole body.
distractors: Arterial blood provides the other concentration in the equation.
One local vein does not represent average whole-body extraction.
Active muscle has unusually high local extraction and can misrepresent the body.

questions.stem: Why is 1500 used to calculate rate from the number of small squares between R waves at 25 mm/s?
options: It is the number of 1-mm squares passing in one minute.
It is the number of millimetres in one normal cardiac cycle.
It is the electrical voltage calibration in millivolts.
It is the standard number of R waves recorded in one minute.
questions.explanation: At 25 mm/s, the paper travels 25 × 60 = 1500 mm per minute. Dividing these 1500 small squares by squares per beat yields beats per minute.
distractors: The distance travelled per cycle varies with RR duration.
Vertical voltage is calibrated at 10 mm per mV.
A person’s actual heart rate is not fixed at 1500 beats per minute.

questions.stem: A patient with massive haemorrhage remains severely hypotensive after blood volume is completely restored. Which stage fits?
options: Early compensated hypovolaemic shock with intact reflexes.
Irreversible shock after extensive tissue injury.
Postural hypotension from remaining upright.
Transient vasovagal faint without major tissue damage.
questions.explanation: Severe myocardial, neural and microvascular damage may prevent recovery even after the original blood-volume loss has been corrected.
distractors: Compensated shock should retain useful mechanisms for pressure support.
Postural hypotension should depend on standing and impaired compensation.
An uncomplicated faint generally improves rapidly when lying flat.

questions.section: 5. Hormones that act on the circulation
questions.stem: After a period of low blood volume, aldosterone secretion increases. Which effect is most important over the following hours to days?
options: Greater renal sodium loss with accompanying water loss.
Immediate electrical acceleration of the intrinsic cardiac pacemaker.
Greater renal sodium retention with accompanying water retention.
Immediate widening of resistance vessels across the circulation.
questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases renal Na⁺ retention, and water follows, helping restore circulating volume over time.
distractors: Sodium and water loss are opposite to aldosterone’s action.
Direct pacemaker acceleration is an autonomic effect, not its main role.
Its principal effect is renal volume conservation, not universal vasodilation.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has a nearly normal arterial pressure but cold skin and reduced urine output. What is the best conclusion?
options: Normal pressure excludes significant shock.
Low perfusion can coexist with normal pressure.
Cardiac output must be above its pre-bleeding level.
Blood flow to all organs must remain normal.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic arteriolar constriction can maintain arterial pressure despite reduced cardiac output and poor perfusion of some tissues.
distractors: Shock is defined by inadequate tissue perfusion, not one pressure value.
Haemorrhage reduces venous return and usually lowers output.
Flow can be redistributed away from skin and kidneys.

questions.stem: Why can chronic widespread alveolar hypoxia lead to pulmonary hypertension?
options: Persistent hypoxia opens every pulmonary capillary without resistance.
Persistent hypoxic constriction increases lung resistance.
Widespread hypoxia lowers pulmonary vascular smooth-muscle tone.
Chronic hypoxia eliminates blood passing through the lungs.
questions.explanation: When hypoxic constriction affects much of the lung, cumulative resistance rises and pulmonary arterial pressure can increase.
distractors: Recruitment is a different response that lowers resistance.
The lecture explicitly associates hypoxia with pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Lung flow generally continues but faces increased resistance.

questions.section: 6. Why does measured BP depend on whether the arm is above or below the heart?
questions.stem: A sphygmomanometer cuff is held substantially below heart level. How is its pressure reading affected by gravity?
options: It reads falsely low because of reduced hydrostatic pressure.
It reads falsely high because of added hydrostatic pressure.
It is unaffected because arterial vessels have valves.
It measures venous instead of arterial pressure.
questions.explanation: A measurement site below the heart has extra hydrostatic pressure, making the reading higher than heart-level pressure.
distractors: Above-heart placement would give a falsely lower reading.
Arteries do not have the venous valves needed to cancel gravity.
The cuff still estimates arterial pressure.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: Once local metabolic dilation restores an organ’s blood flow, what prevents dilation from continuing unchecked?
options: The restored flow removes oxygen from the tissue cells.
The restored flow causes a sustained rise in local lactate.
The restored flow clears accumulated dilator metabolites.
The restored flow abolishes vessel-wall smooth muscle.
questions.explanation: The dilators exist because flow was too low for demand. Once flow matches demand, they are washed away as fast as they are made, so the arterioles regain their tone. This negative feedback stops dilation running away.
distractors: Restored delivery generally improves tissue oxygen availability.
Sustained lactate accumulation would favour continued dilation.
Vascular smooth muscle remains present and functional.

questions.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
questions.stem: A graph of organ flow against perfusion pressure is almost flat over a middle range but slopes downward at very low pressures. Why?
options: The arterioles reach their maximal dilation at low pressure.
The arterioles reach their maximal constriction at low pressure.
The heart stops driving any pressure into the organ.
The veins become the principal resistance at low pressure.
questions.explanation: Once arterioles are fully dilated, they cannot reduce resistance further, so flow decreases as pressure falls.
distractors: Maximal constriction occurs in response to rising pressure, not very low pressure.
A downward slope does not mean perfusion pressure is zero.
Venous vessels do not replace arterioles as the chief resistance site.

questions.section: 8. Clinical significance of conduction disturbances
questions.stem: A ventricular impulse occurs independently of atrial excitation after complete AV conduction block. What has happened?
options: The SA node has increased its firing rate.
The aortic valves transmit an alternate impulse.
Atrial excitation now travels directly through the lungs.
A subsidiary escape pacemaker has taken over.
questions.explanation: Complete AV block prevents atrial impulses from reaching ventricles; a slower escape pacemaker may maintain ventricular rhythm.
distractors: Faster atrial activity alone cannot restore complete AV conduction.
Valves do not propagate cardiac electrical impulses.
The lungs do not provide an alternative physiological conduction path.

questions.stem: A burn patient presents with shock and an initially high haematocrit. What explains the contrast with recent whole-blood haemorrhage?
options: Burns selectively destroy red cells circulating in blood.
Burns produce increased circulating volume despite shock.
Burns cause immediate erythropoietin-driven erythrocytosis.
Plasma leakage leaves intravascular red cells concentrated.
questions.explanation: Severe burns can cause plasma to leak through damaged skin while red cells remain, producing haemoconcentration and raised haematocrit.
distractors: Selective red-cell destruction would tend to lower red-cell concentration.
Plasma loss reduces rather than increases effective circulating volume.
Erythropoiesis is much too slow to explain this early result.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.stem: The jugular venous 'c' wave is chiefly linked to which event?
options: Rapid emptying of the right atrium.
Passive systemic venous filling late in systole.
Systolic bulging of the tricuspid valve.
Right atrial contraction immediately before QRS.
questions.explanation: Early right ventricular contraction can bulge the shut tricuspid valve toward the right atrium, contributing to the c wave.
distractors: Rapid atrial emptying contributes to the y descent.
Venous filling behind a closed tricuspid valve makes the v wave.
Right atrial systole generates the a wave.

questions.section: 5. Orthostatic (postural) hypotension
questions.stem: After three minutes upright, pressure changes from 126/82 to 104/77 mmHg. How is this classified using the chapter criterion?
options: No orthostatic hypotension because diastolic pressure fell only 5 mmHg.
No orthostatic hypotension because final systolic pressure exceeds 100 mmHg.
Orthostatic hypotension because systolic pressure fell 22 mmHg.
Orthostatic hypotension only if both pressures fall by 20 mmHg.
questions.explanation: A sustained systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg within three minutes satisfies the criterion.
distractors: The systolic threshold is met even when the diastolic threshold is not.
The diagnostic threshold concerns the change, not a fixed final pressure.
The definition does not require both components to fall by 20 mmHg.

questions.chapter: Chapter 1 — Introduction to the Heart and Circulation
questions.stem: When both atrioventricular valves are open and semilunar valves are shut, which process predominates?
options: Rapid ventricular ejection into the aorta.
Ventricular filling during diastole.
Closure of the outflow valves at end systole.
Isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
questions.explanation: With ventricular pressure below atrial pressure, AV valves open and blood enters relaxed ventricles while semilunar valves remain closed.
distractors: Ejection requires open semilunar valves.
Outflow valve closure happens near the start of ventricular relaxation.
Isovolumetric contraction occurs after AV valves close.

questions.stem: Following regional node removal, a patient develops persistent firm limb swelling. What explains it?
options: Raised arterial oxygen causes tightness.
Systolic ejection fraction necessarily becomes reduced.
Protein accumulation after failed lymph drainage.
Excess venous flow clears local proteins.
questions.explanation: Lymphatic obstruction impairs removal of interstitial proteins and fluid, leading over time to persistent, often non-pitting swelling.
distractors: Oxygen delivery is not the main mechanism.
Cardiac ejection fraction need not be abnormal.
Impaired lymph drainage prevents, rather than accelerates, interstitial protein removal.

questions.section: 8. Basic rhythm assessment (supplementary)
questions.stem: Which feature most reliably distinguishes first-degree AV block from second-degree AV block in the chapter’s basic ECG classification?
options: Both have identical PR intervals on each beat.
Both show independent P-wave and QRS rhythms.
First-degree conducts every P; second-degree drops some.
First-degree lacks P waves; second-degree lacks QRS complexes.
questions.explanation: First-degree block delays conduction but retains a QRS after every P wave. In second-degree block, at least some atrial impulses fail to produce QRS complexes.
distractors: Second-degree block is defined by intermittent failed conduction, not identical PR intervals.
Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms indicate complete third-degree block.
Both conditions can show P waves and QRS complexes on the trace.

questions.stem: A blood-pressure reading is 132/84 mmHg. What is the pulse pressure?
options: 36 mmHg.
44 mmHg.
48 mmHg.
40 mmHg.
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure equals systolic minus diastolic: 132 − 84 = 48 mmHg. It measures the pressure swing between systole and diastole.
distractors: Thirty-six is below the arithmetic difference.
Forty-four is four mmHg below the difference.
Forty does not equal 132 minus 84.

questions.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
questions.stem: Under the Frank–Starling law, why does greater ventricular filling strengthen systolic force?
options: Reduced preload stimulates immediate calcium extrusion.
Stretch of myocardial fibres strengthens contraction.
Lower venous return increases sarcomere overlap.
Higher afterload increases systemic venous return.
questions.explanation: Within the physiological range, more end-diastolic filling stretches fibres and increases developed contraction force and stroke volume.
distractors: Calcium extrusion is related to relaxation, not the primary stretch mechanism.
Lower venous return reduces ventricular fibre stretch.
Afterload is a separate determinant of ejection.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: A corrected QT interval is 0.46 s. Relative to the upper limit shown in the ECG diagram, how should it be described?
options: Below the displayed upper limit of 0.40 s.
Exactly equal to the displayed upper limit of 0.46 s.
Above the displayed upper limit of 0.44 s.
Within the displayed upper limit of 0.50 s.
questions.explanation: The annotated ECG slide gives a QTc upper limit of 0.44 s. A QTc of 0.46 s exceeds that displayed threshold by 0.02 s.
distractors: The diagram uses 0.44 s for QTc; 0.40 s is part of its uncorrected QT range.
The observed value of 0.46 s is not the stated threshold.
The annotated diagram does not give 0.50 s as its QTc upper limit.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
simulation.stem: A severe rise in intracranial pressure produces systemic hypertension with reflex bradycardia. What is this response?
options: Lung hypoxia reflex.
Atrial stretch reflex.
Bainbridge reflex.
Cushing reflex.
simulation.explanation: The Cushing response reflects brainstem ischaemia driving systemic hypertension, with baroreflex-mediated bradycardia. Brain perfusion is threatened as raised intracranial pressure compresses cerebral vessels.
distractors: Pulmonary hypoxic vasoconstriction is a local lung response.
Atrial stretch does not explain raised ICP-driven hypertension.
Bainbridge responds to increased atrial filling.

simulation.stem: Which pressure relationship helps prevent fluid accumulation in normal pulmonary alveoli?
options: Pulmonary capillary pressure consistently exceeds systemic arterial pressure.
Absence of plasma proteins in pulmonary capillaries.
Relatively low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.
Higher alveolar protein pressure than in capillary plasma.
simulation.explanation: Low pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure relative to plasma oncotic forces helps minimise filtration into air spaces.
distractors: Pulmonary capillary pressure is much lower than systemic arterial pressure.
Plasma proteins contribute the inward oncotic force.
Alveolar spaces normally contain little free fluid and protein.

simulation.stem: A cuff that is far too small is used on a large upper arm. Which measurement error is likely?
options: No systematic effect on cuff pressure.
An undersized cuff gives a falsely high reading.
Only diastolic pressure becomes unmeasurable.
Falsely low BP from excessive arterial unloading.
simulation.explanation: An undersized cuff transmits pressure poorly around a large arm and commonly overestimates measured pressure.
distractors: Cuff size materially affects readings.
Both systolic and diastolic measurements may be distorted.
A small cuff usually overestimates rather than underestimates BP.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
simulation.stem: The CSF volume is about 150 mL and production is 550 mL/day. Approximately how many complete turnovers occur per day?
options: About 4.
About 2.
About 1.
About 6.
simulation.explanation: Dividing daily production by total CSF volume gives 550/150 ≈ 3.7 turnovers each day.
distractors: Two turnovers would require about 300 mL/day.
One turnover would represent only about 150 mL/day.
Six turnovers would correspond to around 900 mL/day.

simulation.stem: Increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure while other Starling forces stay unchanged tends to produce what?
options: Decreased outward fluid filtration.
More fluid filtration into tissues.
Reversal of lymphatic flow.
Increased plasma oncotic attraction.
simulation.explanation: A higher capillary hydrostatic force favours filtration across the microvascular wall toward tissue. Raising venous pressure is one way to produce this hydrostatic change.
distractors: The pressure favours outward, not reduced, filtration.
Lymphatic flow generally responds to excess tissue fluid rather than reversing.
Plasma oncotic pressure does not automatically increase.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
simulation.stem: A patient develops cardiac tamponade. Why can stroke volume fall despite a normal blood volume?
options: Tamponade increases functional ventricular compliance.
Tamponade directly raises venous return above normal.
The aortic valve cannot open due solely to a high heart rate.
High pericardial pressure restricts ventricular filling.
simulation.explanation: Elevated intrapericardial pressure limits end-diastolic filling and preload, reducing stroke volume. The restricted ventricular volume prevents an adequate Frank–Starling response.
distractors: Tamponade reduces the ability of ventricles to expand.
Venous return and effective filling become impaired.
Valvular opening depends on pressure, but reduced preload is the central problem.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: Arterial pressure inside an arteriole is unchanged, but pressure in its surrounding tissue rises. What happens to transmural pressure?
options: It decreases because the pressure difference narrows.
It increases because the pressure difference widens.
It becomes identical to intravascular arterial pressure.
It remains fixed because arterial pressure is unchanged.
simulation.explanation: Transmural pressure equals internal pressure minus surrounding tissue pressure; increasing the latter reduces the difference.
distractors: A higher external pressure reduces, rather than widens, the difference.
It equals internal pressure only when external pressure is zero.
Transmural pressure depends on both internal and external pressure.

simulation.stem: A severely underperfused patient begins breathing rapidly, although the lungs were initially healthy. What drives this change?
options: Increased aerobic ATP production stimulates breathing.
Suppression of the peripheral chemoreceptors stimulates breathing.
Lactic acidosis stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.
High tissue oxygen content increases respiratory drive.
simulation.explanation: Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery promotes anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. The resulting acidemia can stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors and increase ventilation; reduced oxygen delivery alone is not equivalent to low arterial oxygen tension.
distractors: Aerobic metabolism is limited by inadequate oxygen delivery.
Chemoreceptor stimulation, rather than suppression, promotes respiration.
Excess oxygen is not the initiating problem in shock.

simulation.stem: How does local hypoxia affect most systemic arterioles versus pulmonary arterioles?
options: Systemic vessels constrict while pulmonary vessels dilate.
Both primarily constrict to lower oxygen delivery.
Both remain relatively insensitive to tissue oxygen.
Systemic vessels dilate; pulmonary vessels constrict.
simulation.explanation: Systemic hypoxic tissues commonly dilate to improve supply, whereas low alveolar oxygen constricts adjacent pulmonary arterioles to improve ventilation–perfusion matching.
distractors: The response directions have been reversed.
Systemic tissues usually need increased flow in hypoxia.
Oxygen tension influences both beds, but their dominant local responses differ.

simulation.stem: A pressure tracing shows atrial contraction shortly after an ECG P wave and ventricular contraction shortly after QRS. What principle explains both delays?
options: Electrical excitation normally precedes the mechanical response of cardiac muscle.
Mechanical contraction normally finishes before electrical activation begins in the chamber.
The T wave must occur before either chamber can begin contraction.
Atrial and ventricular pressures directly create the corresponding ECG waves.
simulation.explanation: The electrical depolarisation that activates cardiac muscle precedes its force development. P precedes atrial systole, and QRS precedes ventricular systole.
distractors: This reverses the normal electrical-to-mechanical sequence.
The T wave reflects ventricular electrical recovery, after ventricular depolarisation.
Pressure changes follow electrical activation and are not what skin ECG leads measure.

simulation.stem: What extra perspective do the chest leads V1–V6 add to the standard limb-lead views?
options: They replace voltage measurement with intracardiac pressure.
They remove the need to record the frontal electrical plane.
They isolate atrial electrical activity from ventricular activity.
They show cardiac electrical vectors in the horizontal plane.
simulation.explanation: The limb leads provide frontal-plane views, while the precordial leads examine the same heart from different points around the horizontal plane.
distractors: Chest leads, like limb leads, still record surface electrical potentials.
Frontal and horizontal views complement rather than replace one another.
Both sets of leads record combined cardiac electrical events.

simulation.stem: During progressive shock, capillary hydrostatic pressure paradoxically rises while systemic arterial pressure is falling. Which microvascular pattern best explains it?
options: Precapillary constriction with freely draining venules.
Increased venular drainage with reduced capillary entry.
Open capillary entry with constricted venules.
Precapillary constriction with widened venous outlets.
simulation.explanation: With capillary entry relatively open but venular outflow restricted, blood stagnates and local capillary pressure rises, driving fluid into the interstitium.
distractors: Lower entry with free outflow would not cause the described stasis.
Greater drainage would reduce rather than increase local stagnation.
Both reduced entry and improved drainage favour lower capillary pressure.

simulation.stem: Lead II has an upright QRS while aVR has a downward QRS during the same beat. What best explains the difference?
options: Each lead projects the same electrical vector onto a different axis.
One lead measures depolarisation and the other repolarisation.
The two leads record different mechanical contractions.
Atrial and ventricular activity alternate between the leads on each beat.
simulation.explanation: A lead is a directional electrical view. The normal mean ventricular depolarisation vector points generally towards Lead II and away from aVR.
distractors: Both QRS complexes represent ventricular depolarisation, despite opposite polarity.
Both leads sample the electrical activity of the same heartbeat.
Lead orientation does not change the sequence of atrial and ventricular activation.

simulation.stem: A patient with marked polycythaemia has elevated haematocrit. What is the expected direct effect on systemic flow resistance?
options: Lower viscosity and lower total vascular resistance.
Higher viscosity and lower resistance.
Higher viscosity and higher resistance.
Lower viscosity and higher resistance.
simulation.explanation: More red cells increase blood viscosity and consequently vascular resistance, raising the heart's workload.
distractors: Both properties generally increase, not decrease.
Higher viscosity raises resistance rather than lowering it.
Lower viscosity does not follow from higher haematocrit.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: A resting muscle suddenly becomes active while systemic arterial pressure stays steady. What most directly increases its blood supply?
options: Its large veins reduce their compliance.
Its arteries increase their driving pressure.
Its local arterioles reduce their resistance.
Its local capillaries develop stronger contractions.
simulation.explanation: Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. With arterial pressure unchanged, the only way to get more flow is lower resistance, and the resistance that tissues control is in their arterioles. Metabolites from the working muscle relax those arterioles.
distractors: Vein compliance mainly affects stored volume, not the main resistance to flow.
The stem states that systemic arterial pressure remains steady.
Capillaries lack the smooth muscle needed for this response.

simulation.stem: At one instant, Lead I records +0.4 mV and Lead III records −0.2 mV. What must Lead II record?
options: −0.2 mV, from using the third lead alone.
+0.6 mV, from adding their magnitudes.
+0.2 mV, from adding the signed voltages.
−0.6 mV, from subtracting the two values.
simulation.explanation: Einthoven’s law is V(II) = V(I) + V(III). Therefore +0.4 + (−0.2) = +0.2 mV at the same instant.
distractors: Lead II is obtained by combining the two measured limb-lead voltages.
The negative sign of Lead III must be retained in the sum.
This reverses the sign of the result rather than adding the signed voltages.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: A region of heart muscle starts working harder. Which local product of its own metabolism helps increase its blood flow?
options: Serotonin released by nearby platelets.
Angiotensin II formed in the blood.
Noradrenaline from sympathetic nerves.
Adenosine formed as ATP is used up.
simulation.explanation: Working muscle uses ATP faster, and its breakdown products (adenosine, ADP, AMP) build up and dilate the local arterioles. Flow rises in proportion to how hard the tissue works, which is why the heart relies so heavily on this.
distractors: Platelet serotonin constricts vessels, and it comes from platelets, not from the working muscle.
Angiotensin II is a circulating constrictor, not a product of the muscle’s metabolism.
Noradrenaline is a nerve transmitter that mainly constricts arterioles via α₁ receptors.

simulation.stem: What physiological purpose is served by slow conduction through the AV node?
options: It prevents the impulse from ever reaching the ventricular myocardium.
It ensures ventricles eject before the atria contract.
It allows the aortic valve to remain open during atrial systole.
It allows atrial contraction to finish ventricular filling.
simulation.explanation: The AV delay separates atrial and ventricular activation so atrial systole can augment ventricular filling before ventricular systole.
distractors: Normal impulses subsequently travel through His and Purkinje fibres.
The sequence is atrial activation before ventricular activation.
The aortic valve remains closed during ordinary atrial systole.

simulation.stem: Which statement best reflects the updated interpretation of capillary fluid balance?
options: The glycocalyx regulates filtration; lymph returns excess fluid.
Lymphatic vessels play no role when hydrostatic pressure is normal.
Most capillaries continuously reabsorb nearly all filtered fluid at their venous ends.
Interstitial proteins do not affect exchange at any capillary.
simulation.explanation: The revised Starling model includes the glycocalyx and emphasises that sustained net filtration is normally cleared by lymphatics.
distractors: Lymphatic return remains vital even at normal pressures.
The classical arterial filtration–venous reabsorption picture overstates sustained reabsorption.
Protein distributions can influence effective oncotic gradients.

simulation.stem: Minutes after a severe allergic exposure, a patient's pressure drops with generalised swelling. Which vascular action is most relevant?
options: Histamine-related dilatation with increased capillary permeability.
Generalised constriction with reduced capillary permeability.
Increased myocardial pump function with reduced venous capacitance.
Selective haemorrhage into the gastrointestinal tract.
simulation.explanation: Anaphylaxis releases mediators including histamine that widen vessels and increase capillary leakage, reducing effective perfusion.
distractors: Anaphylaxis typically causes dilation and increased leak.
Higher pump performance would not explain the sudden widespread leakage.
Occult bleeding is not the primary allergic vascular mechanism.

simulation.stem: How does normal inspiration tend to assist systemic venous return?
options: It increases right atrial pressure and reduces abdominal pressure.
It closes all systemic venous valves simultaneously.
It increases peripheral venous capacitance until return stops.
Lower chest pressure draws venous blood toward the heart.
simulation.explanation: Inspiration decreases intrathoracic pressure and promotes a pressure gradient drawing blood from peripheral veins to the thorax.
distractors: Lower rather than higher thoracic pressure assists inflow.
Venous valves do not all close in inspiration.
Return is generally supported rather than abolished.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: An exercising leg receives increased blood flow while its muscle continues contracting. What is this response called?
options: Active hyperaemia driven by ongoing tissue metabolism.
Reactive hyperaemia following a temporary flow block.
Baroreflex vasodilation after systemic arterial pressure rises.
Autoregulation that holds its flow at rest level.
simulation.explanation: Active hyperaemia is the rise in flow while a tissue is working: its metabolites dilate the arterioles for as long as activity continues. Reactive hyperaemia is the surge after a blockage is released.
distractors: Reactive hyperaemia is a surge after an obstruction ends.
The increase originates largely from local demand, not a pressure-rise baroreflex.
The flow rises above baseline rather than staying constant.

simulation.stem: Why does persistent lactic acidosis make circulatory shock harder to reverse?
options: It prevents further fluid filtration from capillaries.
It depresses contraction and catecholamine responses.
It directly restores aerobic ATP production.
It increases ventricular force and vascular responsiveness.
simulation.explanation: Acidosis from anaerobic metabolism weakens cardiac pumping and reduces vascular response to catecholamines, undermining compensation.
distractors: Acidosis does not reliably prevent fluid movement into tissues.
Aerobic ATP generation still requires oxygen.
Acidosis impairs rather than strengthens these functions.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: Which of these locally released substances dilates arterioles?
options: Histamine
Endothelin-1
Serotonin
Angiotensin II
simulation.explanation: Histamine, released from mast cells in injury and allergy, relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle (via H₂ receptors) and makes capillaries leakier, which is why inflamed tissue turns red and swollen.
distractors: Endothelin-1 from the endothelium is one of the most powerful constrictors known.
Serotonin from activated platelets constricts the injured vessel to limit bleeding.
Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and raises resistance.

simulation.stem: An ECG machine runs at 25 mm/s. How much time passes while the paper advances by 1 mm horizontally?
simulation.explanation: At a speed of 25 mm each second, 1 mm represents 1/25 s = 0.04 s, the duration of one small horizontal grid square.
distractors: 0.10 s does not correspond to a 1-mm horizontal square at this speed.
0.50 s would occupy 12.5 small squares.
0.20 s is the time represented by one 5-mm large square.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
simulation.stem: A cerebral vessel ruptures and blood enters brain tissue. Which type of cerebrovascular event is present?
options: Cerebral hypoglycaemia.
Embolic ischaemia.
Thrombotic ischaemia.
Haemorrhagic stroke.
simulation.explanation: Haemorrhagic stroke results from rupture of a vessel, whereas ischaemic stroke results from interrupted arterial supply.
distractors: Hypoglycaemia causes global dysfunction rather than vessel rupture.
Embolism blocks flow rather than directly representing vessel rupture.
Thrombosis obstructs an artery instead of rupturing it.

simulation.stem: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL and an end-systolic volume of 55 mL. What is its stroke volume?
options: 75 mL.
55 mL.
simulation.explanation: Stroke volume is EDV minus ESV, so 130 − 55 = 75 mL per beat.
distractors: One hundred thirty mL is end-diastolic volume.
Fifty-five mL is end-systolic volume.
Adding EDV and ESV does not give stroke volume.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
simulation.stem: How does CSF substantially reduce the effective weight of the brain?
options: It increases the brain's intrinsic density.
It provides buoyant support against gravity.
It reduces blood volume to near zero.
It directly reduces the brain's oxygen consumption.
simulation.explanation: Immersion provides buoyancy, reducing the brain's effective supported weight from roughly 1400–1500 g to around 50 g.
distractors: The tissue density does not increase to create buoyancy.
Brain blood volume remains substantial.
Lower oxygen consumption does not explain mechanical support.

simulation.stem: Why is 1500 used to calculate rate from the number of small squares between R waves at 25 mm/s?
options: It is the number of 1-mm squares passing in one minute.
It is the number of millimetres in one normal cardiac cycle.
It is the electrical voltage calibration in millivolts.
It is the standard number of R waves recorded in one minute.
simulation.explanation: At 25 mm/s, the paper travels 25 × 60 = 1500 mm per minute. Dividing these 1500 small squares by squares per beat yields beats per minute.
distractors: The distance travelled per cycle varies with RR duration.
Vertical voltage is calibrated at 10 mm per mV.
A person’s actual heart rate is not fixed at 1500 beats per minute.

simulation.stem: A patient with massive haemorrhage remains severely hypotensive after blood volume is completely restored. Which stage fits?
options: Early compensated hypovolaemic shock with intact reflexes.
Irreversible shock after extensive tissue injury.
Postural hypotension from remaining upright.
Transient vasovagal faint without major tissue damage.
simulation.explanation: Severe myocardial, neural and microvascular damage may prevent recovery even after the original blood-volume loss has been corrected.
distractors: Compensated shock should retain useful mechanisms for pressure support.
Postural hypotension should depend on standing and impaired compensation.
An uncomplicated faint generally improves rapidly when lying flat.

simulation.stem: A bleeding patient has a nearly normal arterial pressure but cold skin and reduced urine output. What is the best conclusion?
options: Normal pressure excludes significant shock.
Low perfusion can coexist with normal pressure.
Cardiac output must be above its pre-bleeding level.
Blood flow to all organs must remain normal.
simulation.explanation: Sympathetic arteriolar constriction can maintain arterial pressure despite reduced cardiac output and poor perfusion of some tissues.
distractors: Shock is defined by inadequate tissue perfusion, not one pressure value.
Haemorrhage reduces venous return and usually lowers output.
Flow can be redistributed away from skin and kidneys.

simulation.stem: Why can chronic widespread alveolar hypoxia lead to pulmonary hypertension?
options: Persistent hypoxia opens every pulmonary capillary without resistance.
Persistent hypoxic constriction increases lung resistance.
Widespread hypoxia lowers pulmonary vascular smooth-muscle tone.
Chronic hypoxia eliminates blood passing through the lungs.
simulation.explanation: When hypoxic constriction affects much of the lung, cumulative resistance rises and pulmonary arterial pressure can increase.
distractors: Recruitment is a different response that lowers resistance.
The lecture explicitly associates hypoxia with pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Lung flow generally continues but faces increased resistance.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: Once local metabolic dilation restores an organ’s blood flow, what prevents dilation from continuing unchecked?
options: The restored flow removes oxygen from the tissue cells.
The restored flow causes a sustained rise in local lactate.
The restored flow clears accumulated dilator metabolites.
The restored flow abolishes vessel-wall smooth muscle.
simulation.explanation: The dilators exist because flow was too low for demand. Once flow matches demand, they are washed away as fast as they are made, so the arterioles regain their tone. This negative feedback stops dilation running away.
distractors: Restored delivery generally improves tissue oxygen availability.
Sustained lactate accumulation would favour continued dilation.
Vascular smooth muscle remains present and functional.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 16 — Local Control of Blood Flow
simulation.stem: A graph of organ flow against perfusion pressure is almost flat over a middle range but slopes downward at very low pressures. Why?
options: The arterioles reach their maximal dilation at low pressure.
The arterioles reach their maximal constriction at low pressure.
The heart stops driving any pressure into the organ.
The veins become the principal resistance at low pressure.
simulation.explanation: Once arterioles are fully dilated, they cannot reduce resistance further, so flow decreases as pressure falls.
distractors: Maximal constriction occurs in response to rising pressure, not very low pressure.
A downward slope does not mean perfusion pressure is zero.
Venous vessels do not replace arterioles as the chief resistance site.

simulation.stem: A burn patient presents with shock and an initially high haematocrit. What explains the contrast with recent whole-blood haemorrhage?
options: Burns selectively destroy red cells circulating in blood.
Burns produce increased circulating volume despite shock.
Burns cause immediate erythropoietin-driven erythrocytosis.
Plasma leakage leaves intravascular red cells concentrated.
simulation.explanation: Severe burns can cause plasma to leak through damaged skin while red cells remain, producing haemoconcentration and raised haematocrit.
distractors: Selective red-cell destruction would tend to lower red-cell concentration.
Plasma loss reduces rather than increases effective circulating volume.
Erythropoiesis is much too slow to explain this early result.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
simulation.stem: The jugular venous 'c' wave is chiefly linked to which event?
options: Rapid emptying of the right atrium.
Passive systemic venous filling late in systole.
Systolic bulging of the tricuspid valve.
Right atrial contraction immediately before QRS.
simulation.explanation: Early right ventricular contraction can bulge the shut tricuspid valve toward the right atrium, contributing to the c wave.
distractors: Rapid atrial emptying contributes to the y descent.
Venous filling behind a closed tricuspid valve makes the v wave.
Right atrial systole generates the a wave.

Closure of the outflow valves at end systole.
Isovolumetric ventricular contraction.

simulation.stem: Under the Frank–Starling law, why does greater ventricular filling strengthen systolic force?
options: Reduced preload stimulates immediate calcium extrusion.
Stretch of myocardial fibres strengthens contraction.
Lower venous return increases sarcomere overlap.
Higher afterload increases systemic venous return.

questions.stem: An ECG marker is placed at the beginning of the P wave. Where must the second marker go to measure the PR interval?
options: At the beginning of the T wave.
At the beginning of the QRS complex.
At the end of the ventricular QRS complex.
At the end of the ventricular T wave.
questions.explanation: The PR interval measures from the onset of atrial depolarisation (P-wave onset) to the onset of ventricular depolarisation (QRS onset).
distractors: The start of T occurs after ventricular depolarisation.
Including all of QRS would extend beyond the PR interval.
The end of T is used to mark the end of the QT interval.

questions.stem: Which response becomes particularly important for supporting pressure during sustained rather than momentary upright posture?
options: Renin–angiotensin effects and renal salt retention.
Suppression of aldosterone-driven sodium retention.
Persistent inhibition of all vascular reflexes.
Loss of sympathetic arteriolar responsiveness.
questions.explanation: The rapid baroreflex stabilizes pressure within seconds, while the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system supports longer-term pressure and volume.
distractors: Aldosterone supports sodium retention rather than its suppression.
Baroreflexes remain available during sustained standing.
Loss of arteriolar responsiveness would worsen orthostatic control.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: Why is the normal T wave generally broader than the QRS complex?
options: The T wave covers atrial and ventricular depolarisation together.
Ventricular depolarisation spreads more slowly than repolarisation.
The T wave corresponds to ventricular contraction rather than electricity.
Ventricular repolarisation usually takes longer than its depolarisation.
questions.explanation: The T wave reflects the slower process of ventricular repolarisation, while QRS represents rapid ventricular depolarisation through the conduction system.
distractors: Atrial and ventricular depolarisation are represented mainly by P and QRS.
The statement reverses the usual relative time courses.
The T wave is still an electrical event, not the force of contraction.

questions.stem: A person becomes angry during an argument, and both pulse and pressure rise. Which route can initiate this response?
options: Cortical signals acting through the hypothalamus on autonomic centres.
Atrial filling signals acting through the kidneys on increased urine output.
Cerebral CSF signals acting through the ventricles on the heart.
Platelet serotonin acting through capillaries on cardiac pacing.
questions.explanation: Emotions such as anger begin in the cortex. The cortex drives the hypothalamus, which excites the vasomotor centre, raising sympathetic output so heart rate and blood pressure rise.
distractors: Renal volume control is too slow and not the primary emotional route.
The CSF pathways do not directly account for this autonomic response.
Platelet serotonin is a local vascular constrictor, not the main emotional signal.

questions.stem: Why can vision fail before consciousness during strong positive acceleration?
options: Retinal perfusion falls as blood shifts toward the feet.
The retina receives blood at higher pressure than the heart.
Intracranial pressure exceeds local arterial pressure.
Positive acceleration shifts blood toward the head.
questions.explanation: Positive g causes leg pooling and reduced pressure at eye level, so retinal perfusion can fail before cerebral consciousness.
distractors: Pressure at eye level decreases during positive g.
The mechanism is reduced eye-level arterial perfusion, not an inevitable ICP excess.
Headward blood movement occurs during negative g.

questions.section: 6. What does central venous pressure tell us?
questions.stem: A patient's right ventricular pumping fails and right atrial pressure rises. Which consequence is most likely?
options: A larger pressure gradient for systemic venous return.
Reduced congestion in peripheral systemic veins.
Reduced venous return gradient with congestion.
Complete disappearance of the jugular venous pulse.
questions.explanation: Higher right atrial pressure opposes venous return and transmits backward into systemic veins, causing congestion.
distractors: Higher right atrial pressure reduces the upstream-to-atrial gradient.
Elevated atrial pressure tends to increase congestion.
JVP often becomes elevated rather than disappearing.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly characterises isovolumetric ventricular contraction?
options: All valves closed, ventricular pressure rises, volume fixed.
AV valves open, semilunar valves open, volume rises.
AV valves open, semilunar valves shut, volume falls.
All valves closed, ventricular pressure falls, volume fixed.
questions.explanation: Both ventricles generate rising pressure with all inlet and outlet valves closed, so neither receives nor ejects blood.
distractors: Open valves permit volume exchange.
AV valves do not remain open once ventricular pressure rises above atrial.
Falling pressure describes isovolumetric relaxation, not contraction.

questions.stem: A patient loses substantial albumin into urine during kidney disease. What Starling-force change is expected?
options: Increased red-cell viscosity causing filtration.
Reduced capillary permeability everywhere.
Increased plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure promotes oedema.
questions.explanation: Proteinuria reduces circulating albumin and its inward oncotic force, favouring movement of fluid into interstitium.
distractors: Viscosity is not the principal mechanism of protein-loss oedema.
Capillary permeability elsewhere need not decrease.
Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.section: 4. Why are the a, c and v waves separated by x and y descents?
questions.stem: What produces the 'a' wave in a normal jugular venous pulse tracing?
options: Right atrial contraction.
Aortic valve opening.
Rapid ventricular ejection.
Pulmonary valve closure.
questions.explanation: The a wave reflects the rise in right atrial pressure during atrial systole. It occurs immediately before right ventricular contraction.
distractors: Aortic opening is a left ventricular outflow event.
Ventricular ejection is not the primary a-wave mechanism.
Pulmonary closure occurs near end systole.

questions.stem: Why is perfusion of the left ventricular myocardium predominantly diastolic?
options: Ventricular contraction compresses intramural vessels.
The coronary ostia close during ventricular systole.
Aortic flow stops entirely during ventricular diastole.
The left ventricle receives no blood during relaxation.
questions.explanation: High left ventricular wall tension during systole squeezes intramyocardial coronary vessels; relaxation permits better flow.
distractors: Coronary ostia remain open through the cardiac cycle.
Aortic pressure persists during diastole and drives coronary flow.
Coronary flow increases during relaxation rather than disappearing.

questions.stem: Beta-1 adrenergic stimulation generally increases ventricular contractility through which sequence?
options: Blocked ryanodine receptors → larger systolic calcium release.
Increased cAMP/PKA signalling → greater calcium availability.
Increased vagal tone → reduced pacemaker slope → stronger contraction.
Reduced cAMP → less calcium entry → weaker contraction.
questions.explanation: Beta-1 signalling raises cAMP and PKA activity, enhancing calcium entry and cycling for stronger contraction.
distractors: Blocking release channels would reduce systolic calcium release.
Vagal slowing is not the main ventricular inotropic pathway.
Beta-1 stimulation raises, not lowers, cAMP.

questions.section: 9. How can blood flow be measured?
questions.stem: What principle allows an electromagnetic flowmeter to determine vascular flow?
options: Moving conductive blood induces voltage in a magnetic field.
An oxygen content difference equals flow independent of metabolism.
A cuff detects the onset of venous Korotkoff sounds.
A radioactive tracer measures only red-cell lifespan.
questions.explanation: Conducting blood moving through a magnetic field induces a voltage that can be used to estimate its velocity and flow.
distractors: That describes neither the electromagnetic principle nor Fick correctly.
Korotkoff sounds estimate arterial blood pressure, not direct flow.
Tracer approaches are distinct from electromagnetic flow measurement.

questions.stem: A person lying still stands up, then begins walking. What feature makes the calf-muscle pump effective?
options: Venule dilation without pressure gradients.
Capillary contraction during each footstep.
Deep vein compression with one-way valves.
Arterial compression with bidirectional valves.
questions.explanation: Calf contractions compress deep veins, while competent venous valves favour upward flow toward the heart instead of backflow.
distractors: Venous return requires directed pressure gradients, not dilation alone.
Capillaries do not function as contractile muscle pumps.
Arteries do not rely on venous-style one-way valves.

questions.stem: Why may arterial blood pressure rise sharply during severe medullary ischaemia caused by raised intracranial pressure?
options: Direct vasomotor-centre inhibition greatly decreases total sympathetic outflow.
Increased vagal discharge is the main cause of the pressure rise.
Direct vasomotor-centre excitation greatly increases sympathetic outflow.
Increased atrial ANP release is the main cause of the pressure rise.
questions.explanation: Hypoxic, hypercapnic medullary tissue drives a strong sympathetic pressor response to restore cerebral blood flow.
distractors: Inhibition would tend to lower vascular tone and pressure.
Vagal discharge slows the heart and is not the primary pressor mechanism.
ANP favours dilation and volume loss.

questions.section: 4. Low-pressure receptors: sensing how full the circulation is
questions.stem: An atrial stretch receptor fires more during late atrial diastole when venous filling increases. Which receptor type fits best?
options: Type B, reflecting greater atrial filling.
An aortic body receptor, reflecting low oxygen.
A carotid sinus receptor, reflecting arterial stretch.
Type A, reflecting stronger atrial contraction.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies type B atrial receptors as filling-sensitive and more active when the atrial wall is distended.
distractors: Aortic body receptors monitor blood chemistry.
Carotid sinus receptors monitor high-pressure arterial stretch.
Type A activity is linked to atrial systole.

questions.stem: A standard ECG uses ten skin electrodes but produces twelve electrical views. How is this possible?
options: Two extra electrodes inside the heart are automatically activated for recording.
Several leads are calculated from combinations of the same electrode voltages.
Each electrode produces one lead, with two more produced by blood-pressure sensors.
The limb electrodes are relocated to the chest during every cardiac cycle.
questions.explanation: A lead is an electrical viewpoint calculated from one or more electrode potentials, so ten physical contacts can generate twelve different standard recordings.
distractors: Routine twelve-lead ECG does not require intracardiac electrodes.
All twelve are electrical leads; pressure sensors do not generate extra leads.
The limb contacts remain in place during a standard recording.

questions.stem: Why does positioning an accelerating pilot more horizontally improve tolerance to positive g?
options: It shortens the heart-to-brain hydrostatic column.
It increases the distance between the heart and brain.
It directs pooled blood toward the ankles.
It raises the capillary filtration rate in the legs.
questions.explanation: A more horizontal posture decreases the vertical distance over which acceleration reduces pressure toward the head and brain.
distractors: Increasing the vertical distance would worsen the gradient.
Enhanced ankle pooling would reduce central venous return.
Greater dependent filtration would not protect brain perfusion.

questions.section: 1. Why does the body need central control?
questions.stem: Cardiac output falls by 20%, but total peripheral resistance rises by 25%. What happens to mean arterial pressure in the simplified MAP relation?
options: It remains approximately unchanged.
It decreases by approximately one quarter.
It increases by approximately one quarter.
It decreases by approximately one fifth.
questions.explanation: In MAP ≈ CO × TPR, 0.80 × 1.25 = 1.00, so the changes cancel mathematically.
distractors: The combined product does not fall by one quarter.
That ignores the fall in cardiac output.
That ignores the compensatory rise in resistance.

questions.stem: A ventricular depolarisation vector runs almost perpendicular to the viewing axis of a lead. What should that lead record?
options: A small or biphasic ventricular deflection.
A tall downward ventricular deflection.
A tall upright ventricular deflection.
A prolonged ventricular depolarisation interval.
questions.explanation: Only the component of the electrical vector along the lead axis contributes strongly to the deflection; a near-perpendicular vector has a small projection.
distractors: A strongly downward deflection needs a substantial vector component away from the positive pole.
A strongly upright deflection needs a substantial vector component towards the positive pole.
Vector orientation changes amplitude and polarity, not necessarily conduction duration.

questions.stem: A vascular bed has a pressure difference of 80 mmHg and resistance of 20 mmHg·min/L. What is its flow?
options: 2 L/min.
4 L/min.
8 L/min.
3 L/min.
questions.explanation: Flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance: 80/20 = 4 L/min. Increasing resistance with the same pressure difference would lower flow.
distractors: Two L/min would correspond to resistance of 40.
Eight L/min would correspond to resistance of 10.
Three L/min does not fit the given ratio.

questions.section: 4. How the body fights back
questions.stem: Which time course of spontaneous recovery best fits the lecture after bleeding has been stopped?
options: Blood volume in weeks; haemoglobin in hours.
Both volume and haemoglobin fully recover in minutes.
Haemoglobin in 12–72 hours; volume in 4–5 weeks.
Volume in 12–72 hours; haemoglobin in 4–5 weeks.
questions.explanation: Tissue-fluid recruitment and renal retention restore blood volume within roughly 12–72 hours; erythropoietin-driven red-cell recovery requires several weeks.
distractors: The timing of the two processes is reversed.
Neither process replaces major losses within minutes.
Haemoglobin replacement occurs much more slowly than fluid recovery.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.stem: In complete AV dissociation, the right atrium occasionally contracts against a closed tricuspid valve. What JVP abnormality may follow?
options: An isolated giant v wave after every beat.
Intermittent cannon a waves.
A steady nonpulsatile jugular column.
Loss of all visible venous pulsations.
questions.explanation: Unsynchronised atrial contraction against a shut AV valve can produce large intermittent cannon a waves.
distractors: Giant v waves primarily suggest tricuspid regurgitation.
Atrial contractions still cause pressure variations.
Venous pulsations can persist despite AV block.
