questions.explanation: Persistent failure of lymphatic drainage leaves protein-rich fluid in the interstitium, promoting chronic inflammation and fibrosis. This explains why longstanding lymphoedema becomes firm and often non-pitting.
distractors: Rapid reabsorption would tend to reduce swelling and protein accumulation.
Chronic interstitial protein deposition can drive fibrosis despite any venous tone changes.
The chronic fibrosis is linked to sustained lymphatic obstruction, not a brief arterial-pressure change.

questions.section: 4. How the body fights back
questions.stem: Immediately after rapid loss of a large volume of whole blood, haemoglobin concentration is unexpectedly unchanged. Why?
options: Red-cell mass increases enough to compensate.
Plasma enters faster than red cells are lost.
Red cells and plasma were lost together.
Erythropoietin instantly makes new red cells.
questions.explanation: Acute whole-blood loss removes red cells and plasma proportionately, so concentration may remain unchanged before fluid replacement.
distractors: Red-cell mass falls with whole-blood loss.
Early dilution has not yet occurred in this scenario.
Erythropoiesis takes days to weeks, not minutes.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided forward heart failure reports fatigue and produces very little urine. Which mechanism links the two?
options: Elevated venous pressure increases renal filtration.
Reduced systemic perfusion limits muscle and renal blood flow.
Pulmonary congestion causes systemic arteriolar dilation.
Increased left ventricular output stimulates renal water loss.
questions.explanation: Reduced blood ejected from the left heart impairs delivery to skeletal muscle and kidneys, causing fatigue and oliguria.
distractors: Higher venous pressure does not directly improve GFR.
The primary forward mechanism is reduced output, not pulmonary congestion.
The syndrome involves reduced rather than excessive systemic delivery.

questions.stem: A recording shows that cardiac vagal stimulation lowers the firing rate of the sinoatrial node. Which additional effect is expected?
options: Stronger ventricular contraction through beta-1 activation.
Faster impulse conduction through the AV node.
Slower impulse conduction through the AV node.
Faster pacemaker discharge through alpha-1 activation.
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic acetylcholine acts at muscarinic M₂ receptors to slow both SA nodal firing and AV nodal conduction.
distractors: β₁ activation describes sympathetic, not vagal, stimulation.
AV conduction is slowed rather than accelerated by vagal action.
The major cardiac pacemaker effect is not mediated by α₁.

questions.chapter: Chapter 22 — Cerebral Circulation, CSF and the Blood–Brain Barrier
questions.section: 5. The coverings, the ventricles and CSF
questions.stem: A patient has hydrocephalus due to impaired absorption by arachnoid villi without an obstructed ventricular pathway. What type is this?
options: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus.
Obstructive aqueductal hydrocephalus.
Communicating hydrocephalus.
Isolated ventricular haemorrhage.
questions.explanation: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF reaches subarachnoid space but reabsorption is impaired. The ventricular pathway remains open, so the defect is in absorption rather than transit.
distractors: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus results from blocked ventricular drainage.
Aqueductal stenosis is a specific obstruction.
Haemorrhage may contribute to hydrocephalus but is not the classification described.

questions.chapter: Chapter 8 — Measuring Cardiac Output and the Work of the Heart
questions.stem: What conservation principle underlies Fick measurement of cardiac output?
options: Venous oxygen usually matches arterial oxygen content.
Oxygen consumption is independent of blood flow and extraction.
Oxygen use equals flow × arterial–venous oxygen difference.
The heart produces all consumed oxygen internally.
questions.explanation: By mass balance, oxygen uptake across lungs and consumption by tissues equal cardiac output multiplied by arterial–venous oxygen content difference.
distractors: Tissues extract oxygen, so venous content is generally lower.
Extraction and flow together determine total oxygen consumption.
The body consumes oxygen but does not produce it.

questions.stem: What keeps tissue fluid moving through collecting lymph vessels toward the great veins?
options: Valves, muscle movement and lymphatic contractions.
Direct diffusion of whole lymph vessels through tissues.
Constant backflow from the vena cava.
Only the left ventricular ejection pressure.
questions.explanation: One-way valves, skeletal-muscle compression, respiratory movement and lymphatic smooth-muscle contraction promote forward flow. The valves prevent reflux between compressions, making the low-pressure pumping effective.
distractors: Whole vessels do not diffuse through tissues.
Backflow is limited by valves rather than required for transport.
Lymph flow is not driven directly by systemic arterial pressure.

questions.section: 6. Why is vessel radius such a powerful determinant of flow?
questions.stem: An arteriole's radius falls to half its previous value; other variables stay constant. How does its resistance change?
options: By a factor of 2.
By a factor of 4.
By a factor of 8.
A factor of 16.
questions.explanation: Poiseuille resistance varies with 1/r⁴; halving radius raises resistance by 2⁴ = 16. The radius effect is disproportionately large because it is raised to the fourth power.
distractors: A doubling assumes linear radius dependence.
Fourfold assumes a square-law dependence.
Eightfold assumes a cubic rather than fourth-power relation.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided heart failure feels breathless when lying flat but improves after sitting up. Why?
options: Lying flat shifts peripheral blood toward congested lungs.
Lying flat reduces central blood volume.
Sitting up directly increases pulmonary capillary pressure.
Sitting up increases venous return from the legs.
questions.explanation: Supine positioning returns peripheral blood to the thorax; a failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra flow, increasing pulmonary venous congestion.
distractors: Central thoracic volume commonly increases rather than decreases supine.
A higher pulmonary capillary pressure would worsen breathlessness.
Sitting upright tends to reduce thoracic venous return.

questions.stem: A regular rhythm has 24 small squares between adjacent R waves at standard paper speed. Approximately what is the heart rate?
options: 50 beats/min.
80 beats/min.
63 beats/min.
60 beats/min.
questions.explanation: The rate in a regular rhythm is 1500 divided by the R–R separation in small squares: 1500/24 = 62.5 beats/min, approximately 63.
distractors: 50 beats/min corresponds to about 30 small squares between R waves.
80 beats/min corresponds to about 18.75 small squares between R waves.
60 beats/min corresponds to about 25 small squares between R waves.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.section: 4. Why are the a, c and v waves separated by x and y descents?
questions.stem: What does the normal jugular venous 'v' wave mainly represent?
options: Closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve.
Right atrial electrical depolarisation.
Completion of left ventricular ejection.
Atrial filling while tricuspid is closed.
questions.explanation: Systemic venous return fills the right atrium during ventricular systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed, creating the v wave.
distractors: Pulmonary valve closure is near S2.
Atrial depolarisation precedes the a wave.
The v wave is defined by right atrial filling rather than aortic ejection.

questions.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.stem: What is detected by the fingers when palpating the radial pulse?
options: A direct pulse of venous blood into the radial artery.
An arterial wall-distension pressure wave.
Individual red cells striking the wrist.
An electrical signal passing along the endothelium.
questions.explanation: Each ventricular ejection creates an arterial pressure/distension wave that travels along the arteries. This pressure wave moves faster than the bulk blood itself.
distractors: Venous blood does not directly pulse into systemic arteries.
Red cells are not separately felt during palpation.
The palpable pulse is mechanical rather than an electrical conduction wave.

questions.stem: V2 has been placed correctly and V4 is at its usual site. Where should V3 be attached?
options: At the fifth space, midaxillary line.
At the fifth space, anterior axillary line.
At the fourth space, right sternal border.
Halfway between the V2 and V4 electrodes.
questions.explanation: V3 is placed between the already positioned V2 and V4, so the anatomical line between those contacts determines its location.
distractors: The midaxillary line at V4 level is used for V6.
The anterior axillary line at V4 level is used for V5.
The fourth right parasternal position belongs to V1.

questions.section: 4. Waves, segments and intervals: what is the difference?
questions.stem: Using Bazett’s formula, QTc = QT/√RR, what is QTc when QT is 0.36 s and RR is 0.81 s?
options: 0.29 s, because QT is multiplied by RR.
0.32 s, because QT is multiplied by √RR.
0.44 s, because RR is added to QT first.
0.40 s, because QT is divided by 0.90.
questions.explanation: Since √0.81 = 0.90, Bazett’s correction is 0.36/0.90 = 0.40 s. The correction adjusts the observed QT for heart rate.
distractors: Multiplying by RR is not Bazett’s rate-correction formula.
QT should be divided by √RR, not multiplied by it.
Adding QT and RR has no role in the stated equation.

questions.stem: Where is the largest controllable fall in systemic vascular pressure normally produced?
options: Across the venae cavae.
Within the right atrium alone.
Across resistance arterioles.
Across large elastic arteries.
questions.explanation: Small arteries and arterioles provide substantial resistance, producing a major pressure drop from arterial to capillary levels.
distractors: Large veins carry blood at low pressure and resistance.
Right atrial pressure is low but does not create the main distributed arterial drop.
Large elastic arteries conduct flow with relatively small resistance.

questions.stem: Why does the sinoatrial node ordinarily set the heart's rhythm rather than latent pacemakers?
options: Its action potentials last longer than all other cells.
It has the fastest intrinsic depolarisation rate.
It receives oxygen from the pulmonary veins first.
Its cells have the largest ventricular muscle mass.
questions.explanation: The SA node normally reaches threshold fastest and overdrive-suppresses slower latent pacemakers. Faster SA-node impulses normally suppress slower escape pacemakers.
distractors: Action potential duration is not the primary reason for the fastest spontaneous rate.
Coronary perfusion is not determined by pulmonary venous timing.
Pacemaker dominance does not depend on muscle mass.

questions.section: 2. The pathway of cardiac electrical conduction
questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces normal electrical conduction from atria into ventricular myocardium?
options: SA node → Purkinje fibres → AV node → His bundle.
SA node → AV node → His bundle → Purkinje fibres.
AV node → SA node → left ventricle → right atrium.
Purkinje fibres → atria → SA node → AV node.
questions.explanation: The SA node initiates impulses that reach the AV node, traverse the His–bundle branches and Purkinje system, then depolarise ventricles.
distractors: Purkinje fibres come after the AV–His pathway.
The SA node normally initiates atrial excitation.
Ventricular Purkinje fibres conduct after, not before, atrial activation.

questions.chapter: Chapter 1 — Introduction to the Heart and Circulation
questions.stem: Why can coordinated cardiac pumping continue without a new external nerve impulse for every beat?
options: The atrial myocardium conducts only during expiration.
Intrinsic pacemaker cells generate rhythmic impulses.
The sinoatrial node supplies the pressure needed for ejection.
Cardiac cells cannot spontaneously depolarise.
questions.explanation: Specialised cardiac pacemaker cells depolarise spontaneously; autonomic nerves modulate rather than initiate each heartbeat.
distractors: Atrial conduction is not limited to expiration.
The SA node produces electrical impulses, not direct ejection pressure.
Some conducting cells possess spontaneous automaticity.

questions.stem: A patient has near-normal resting cardiac output but very high ventricular filling pressures and pulmonary congestion. Which statement fits best?
options: Heart failure can occur with normal output.
High filling pressure proves adequate pumping.
Heart failure requires reduced ejection fraction.
Normal resting output excludes heart failure.
questions.explanation: Heart failure includes states where output is maintained only at abnormally high filling pressures, causing congestion.
distractors: High filling pressures can be evidence of dysfunction rather than normality.
Diastolic failure can occur with preserved ejection fraction.
A near-normal output can be maintained at harmful filling pressures.

questions.section: 5. Ejection: why blood finally leaves
questions.stem: What event ends isovolumetric contraction and begins ventricular ejection?
options: Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
Atrial contraction briefly increases end-diastolic volume.
Ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.
Ventricular pressure exceeds the outflow artery pressure.
questions.explanation: Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic or pulmonary arterial pressure. The pressure reversal is the immediate mechanical trigger for valve opening.
distractors: This pressure relation opens the AV valves during filling.
Atrial systole precedes isovolumetric contraction.
Lower ventricular than aortic pressure holds the aortic valve closed.

questions.stem: Which pressure difference primarily drives blood back to the right atrium from the body?
options: Aortic systolic minus right ventricular systolic pressure.
Left ventricular systolic minus aortic diastolic pressure.
Systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure.
Pulmonary venous minus pulmonary capillary pressure.
questions.explanation: Venous return depends on the upstream systemic filling pressure relative to right atrial pressure and the resistance to venous return.
distractors: Aortic-right ventricular systolic pressure is not the venous return driving gradient.
That difference is a pulse-pressure-related comparison.
Pulmonary venous pressure does not define systemic venous return.

questions.stem: What can follow when the right ventricle fails to deliver adequate forward flow to the lungs?
options: Pulmonary flow rises despite low right ventricular output.
Less blood reaches the left heart for systemic output.
Systemic tissues receive more oxygen-rich blood immediately.
Left ventricular filling necessarily increases sharply.
questions.explanation: Reduced right ventricular output limits pulmonary flow and subsequent return to the left atrium, compromising left-sided filling and delivery.
distractors: The right heart cannot deliver excess flow when severely failing.
Reduced pulmonary transit cannot raise systemic oxygen delivery.
Less pulmonary venous return tends to decrease left-sided filling.

questions.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
questions.section: 2. Trace the fetal circuit
questions.stem: Where does the ductus arteriosus carry much fetal right ventricular output?
options: Directly from right atrium to left atrium.
From pulmonary trunk into descending aorta.
From left ventricle into hepatic portal vein.
From umbilical vein into inferior vena cava.
questions.explanation: High prenatal pulmonary resistance diverts much right ventricular output through ductus arteriosus into the aorta.
distractors: Right-to-left atrial passage occurs at the foramen ovale.
Left ventricular output does not enter the portal vein.
Umbilical venous diversion occurs at the ductus venosus.

questions.stem: At an otherwise unchanged capillary, how would increased interstitial protein concentration affect fluid movement?
options: It increases protein attraction into the blood compartment.
It strengthens plasma oncotic pressure, reducing filtration.
It lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration.
It strengthens the outward oncotic force favouring filtration.
questions.explanation: More interstitial protein increases interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, tending to pull fluid outward from the capillary and increase filtration.
distractors: Increased proteins outside the capillary attract rather than remove interstitial water.
Plasma protein concentration is held constant; the changed force is interstitial.
A change in interstitial protein does not directly lower capillary pressure.

questions.stem: Electrical stimulation of the medullary pressor area increases arterial pressure. What is the principal neural pathway?
options: Direct stimulation of the carotid sinus sensory fibres.
Inhibition of sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord.
Direct inhibition of firing in the sinoatrial pacemaker.
Excitation of sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The pressor area sends excitatory fibres down to the sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord. More sympathetic output constricts arterioles and veins and speeds and strengthens the heart, so pressure rises.
distractors: Carotid sinus fibres carry sensory information towards the medulla.
Inhibiting sympathetic neurons would tend to lower pressure.
Pressor-area activity does not require direct pacemaker inhibition.

questions.section: 1. Two circulations in one lung
questions.stem: Which pair correctly identifies the lung's respiratory and supporting arterial circulations?
options: Bronchial arteries for gas exchange and coronary arteries for support.
Pulmonary arteries for support and hepatic arteries for gas exchange.
Pulmonary arteries: gas exchange; bronchial arteries: support.
Pulmonary veins for gas exchange and aortic veins for support.
questions.explanation: Pulmonary arteries carry blood for gas exchange, while bronchial arteries from the aorta nourish lung supporting structures.
distractors: Bronchial arteries primarily nourish lung tissue; coronary arteries nourish heart.
The functional roles of pulmonary and bronchial supplies are reversed.
Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood; aortic veins are not a normal supply.

questions.stem: A patient has low circulating volume. Which hormone chiefly increases renal water retention and can constrict vessels at high concentration?
options: Vasopressin, also called ADH.
Atrial natriuretic peptide.
Vasoactive intestinal peptide.
Endothelial prostacyclin.
questions.explanation: ADH promotes renal water conservation and has a vasoconstrictor action when its level is high.
distractors: ANP promotes sodium and water loss.
VIP is a vasodilator rather than a water-retaining hormone.
Prostacyclin dilates vessels and limits platelet aggregation.

questions.stem: Why might severe anaemia produce a cardiac flow murmur despite structurally normal valves?
options: Lower viscosity and increased flow favour turbulence.
Reduced blood volume necessarily closes the aortic valve.
Anaemia markedly increases blood viscosity and suppresses flow.
Anaemia blocks the ventricular conduction system.
questions.explanation: Anaemia lowers viscosity and may increase cardiac output, raising the tendency to turbulent flow and a functional murmur.
distractors: The murmur is not due to forced aortic valve closure.
Anaemia decreases viscosity rather than increasing it.
Conduction block is not the principal mechanism of flow murmurs.

questions.section: 2. Why doesn't blood stop moving during diastole?
questions.stem: During ventricular diastole, what would an increase in peripheral resistance do to the rate of aortic pressure decline if compliance were unchanged?
options: Speed the decline by increasing downstream runoff.
Leave the decline unaffected by downstream resistance.
Slow the decline by reducing downstream runoff.
Reverse arterial flow from capillaries toward the aorta.
questions.explanation: Greater downstream resistance reduces diastolic runoff from the elastic arterial reservoir; at unchanged compliance, aortic pressure falls more slowly.
distractors: Greater resistance normally reduces runoff rather than increasing it.
Diastolic decay depends in part on resistance and arterial compliance.
Higher resistance slows forward runoff but does not reverse normal arterial flow.

simulation.stem: A patient has a sudden rise in arteriolar sympathetic firing with minimal change in cardiac output. Which immediate variable rises most directly?
options: The intrinsic rate of the SA node.
The rate of tissue metabolite clearance.
Total peripheral resistance.
Systemic venous compliance.
simulation.explanation: Arteriolar constriction increases resistance and therefore tends to raise arterial pressure even at stable output.
distractors: SA nodal rate concerns cardiac autonomic effects rather than arteriolar action.
Metabolite clearance depends on local blood flow, not this direct action.
Sympathetic venoconstriction generally reduces venous compliance.

simulation.stem: The R–R separation is four large squares on a regular standard-speed ECG. What is the heart rate?
options: 75 beats/min.
120 beats/min.
60 beats/min.
90 beats/min.
simulation.explanation: At 25 mm/s, a large square equals 0.20 s. Four large squares represent 0.8 s per beat, giving 60/0.8 = 75 beats/min.
distractors: 120 beats/min would require 2.5 large squares.
60 beats/min would require five large squares between R waves.
90 beats/min would require about 3.33 large squares.

simulation.stem: Portal hypertension promotes ascites partly by increasing which force?
options: Plasma oncotic pressure within hepatic capillaries.
Hydrostatic pressure in hepatic sinusoids.
Interstitial lymphatic pumping efficiency.
Arterial oxygen tension in the hepatic vein.
simulation.explanation: Higher sinusoidal hydrostatic pressure increases fluid filtration and hepatic lymph formation; excess can enter the peritoneal cavity.
distractors: Higher plasma oncotic pressure would oppose outward fluid filtration.
Improved lymphatic clearance would tend to oppose accumulation.
Oxygen tension is not the main Starling-force mechanism.

simulation.stem: Which contrast best distinguishes forward failure from backward failure?
options: Forward reduces delivery; backward causes venous congestion.
Forward is venous congestion; backward is low organ blood flow.
Forward indicates excess cardiac output; backward low afterload.
Forward is confined to the right heart; backward to the left.
simulation.explanation: Forward failure describes inadequate delivery to downstream tissues, whereas backward failure describes elevated pressure and congestion upstream of a failing chamber.
distractors: The two effects are reversed in this statement.
Reduced flow and congestion, not excessive output, are the defining patterns.
Either side can produce both forward and backward consequences.

simulation.stem: What directly promotes pulmonary oedema in left-sided backward heart failure?
options: Reduced pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.
Reduced systemic venous pressure throughout the body.
Raised pulmonary venous and capillary pressure.
Raised right atrial pressure without lung congestion.
simulation.explanation: Left ventricular failure increases left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures, driving filtration into the lungs.
distractors: Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure would oppose filtration.
Systemic venous pressure is more closely linked to right-sided failure.
Right atrial pressure alone does not explain pulmonary oedema.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
simulation.stem: Why does the fetal cardiovascular system divert much blood away from the pulmonary circuit before birth?
options: The fetal left ventricle cannot generate arterial pressure.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is exceptionally low before birth.
Umbilical arteries carry already oxygenated blood to the heart.
The placenta oxygenates blood; fetal lungs resist flow.
simulation.explanation: The placenta performs gas exchange before birth; fluid-filled fetal lungs have high resistance, favouring right-to-left shunts.
distractors: The fetal left ventricle contributes significantly to systemic output.
Pulmonary resistance is high before aeration.
Umbilical arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood toward placenta.

simulation.stem: An ECG electrode detects a voltage on the skin even though the impulse originates in the myocardium. What makes this possible?
options: The heart mechanically transmits its pulse to every skin electrode.
The electrodes measure changes in circulating blood pressure.
Cardiac electrical currents spread through conducting body tissues.
The chest electrodes directly contact ventricular muscle fibres.
simulation.explanation: Depolarisation and repolarisation create voltage differences that propagate through the conductive tissues of the body and can be detected at the skin.
distractors: Mechanical pulsation is distinct from electrical potential recorded by ECG electrodes.
Surface ECG electrodes do not directly measure intravascular blood pressure.
The electrodes sit on intact skin, not within the myocardium.

simulation.stem: Heart rate rises from 70 to 80 beats/min while stroke volume stays at 70 mL. By how much does cardiac output increase?
options: By 0.80 litres per minute.
By 0.70 litres per minute.
By about 0.49 litres per minute.
By 1.40 litres per minute.
simulation.explanation: The increase is 10 beats/min × 70 mL/beat = 700 mL/min, or 0.70 L/min.
distractors: 0.80 L/min treats the extra beats as a larger volume.
0.49 L/min does not follow from the given rate change.
1.40 L/min doubles the actual change.

simulation.stem: Most sympathetic constrictor fibres release noradrenaline onto arteriolar smooth muscle. Which receptor mainly mediates constriction?
options: The beta-2 adrenergic receptor on vessels.
The muscarinic M2 receptor.
The endothelial H2 receptor.
The alpha-1 adrenergic receptor.
simulation.explanation: Noradrenaline binds α₁ receptors on arteriolar smooth muscle, raising intracellular Ca²⁺ and contracting the muscle. This raises resistance and arterial pressure.
distractors: β₂ activation typically dilates muscle arterioles.
M₂ receptors mediate vagal slowing of the heart.
H₂ receptors respond to histamine, which dilates arterioles.

simulation.stem: A harsh systolic murmur develops during blood ejection through a narrowed aortic valve. What mechanism explains it?
options: Opening of the aortic valve during ventricular relaxation.
Turbulent forward flow through a stenotic outflow orifice.
Regurgitation through the mitral valve during diastole.
Laminar blood flow through a normal-sized valve.
simulation.explanation: Aortic stenosis accelerates blood through a narrow outlet during systole, causing a turbulent ejection murmur.
distractors: The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure in systole.
Mitral regurgitation usually occurs during systole, not diastole.
Laminar flow through normal valves ordinarily produces no such murmur.

simulation.stem: At 25 mm/s, a PR interval extends across 4.5 small squares. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: 0.24 s, above the stated PR-interval range.
0.09 s, shorter than the stated normal PR-interval range.
0.90 s, above the stated PR-interval range.
0.18 s, inside the stated PR-interval range.
simulation.explanation: The horizontal duration is 4.5 × 0.04 = 0.18 s. This lies within the 0.12–0.20 s interval given in the lecture.
distractors: This is not the product of 4.5 and 0.04 s.
This incorrectly halves the duration obtained from 4.5 small squares.
This incorrectly assigns 0.20 s to each small square.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
simulation.stem: Why does fetal haemoglobin load oxygen effectively at the placental interface?
options: It binds 2,3-BPG more tightly than adult haemoglobin.
Its weaker 2,3-BPG binding increases oxygen affinity.
It is produced without haem groups before birth.
Its iron permanently binds each oxygen molecule.
simulation.explanation: HbF interacts less with 2,3-BPG, shifting its oxygen dissociation curve left and favouring oxygen uptake from maternal blood.
distractors: Stronger 2,3-BPG binding would lower oxygen affinity.
Fetal haemoglobin still contains iron-bearing haem groups.
Oxygen binding is reversible, not permanent.

simulation.stem: During severe hepatic hypoperfusion, cells near the central vein are especially vulnerable to hypoxia. Why?
options: They are located outside the hepatic sinusoidal network.
They are closest to arterial inflow.
They are farthest downstream from the portal triads.
They receive blood with the highest oxygen content.
simulation.explanation: Centrilobular cells receive blood after it has travelled from portal triads, making them less oxygenated and vulnerable.
distractors: Centrilobular hepatocytes remain within the sinusoidal perfusion system.
Oxygenated hepatic arterial inflow enters near the portal triads.
Blood oxygen content generally falls as it traverses sinusoids.

simulation.stem: Following a substantial meal, intestinal blood flow rises for several hours. What primarily drives this response?
options: Global sympathetic constriction of intestinal arteries.
Reduced intestinal metabolism during nutrient absorption.
Complete diversion of portal blood away from liver.
Local metabolic activity and absorptive demand.
simulation.explanation: Postprandial metabolic and absorptive activity promotes local gastrointestinal hyperaemia; the lecture notes it can last about three hours.
distractors: Sympathetic constriction usually opposes the flow increase.
Absorption increases rather than abolishes local work.
Portal flow continues to deliver absorbed substances to liver.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 7 — Cardiac Output and the Frank–Starling Law
simulation.stem: Two Frank–Starling curves are plotted against identical end-diastolic volumes. What does an upward shift of the entire curve usually indicate?
options: Greater contractility at the same preload.
Greater afterload alone with unchanged contractility.
Aortic valve closure earlier in systole.
Lower force development at every fibre length.
simulation.explanation: Positive inotropy raises stroke volume or output at the same filling level, shifting the Frank–Starling function upward.
distractors: Higher afterload tends to impair ejection.
Valve closure timing is not the definition of an upward Starling curve.
Lower force would shift the curve downward, not upward.

simulation.stem: During a stress response, circulating adrenaline dilates vessels in working skeletal muscle while constricting many skin vessels. Why?
options: The muscle vessels lack any adrenergic receptors.
Different vascular beds express different adrenergic receptors.
Skin tissue receives a much lower concentration of adrenaline.
Different vascular beds contain markedly different amounts of plasma.
simulation.explanation: β₂ effects can favour dilation in skeletal muscle, while α₁ effects cause constriction in many skin and gut vessels.
distractors: Muscle vessels respond because they possess adrenergic receptors.
The difference is due mainly to receptor distribution rather than selective circulating delivery.
Plasma volume differences do not explain opposite receptor responses.

simulation.stem: In severe haemorrhagic shock, why does sympathetic constriction of splanchnic vessels help initially?
options: It increases flow to the intestinal mucosa above baseline.
It increases hepatic oxygen extraction to 100%.
It prevents all intestinal ischaemia during shock.
It redistributes flow and mobilises stored venous blood.
simulation.explanation: The splanchnic bed is a large blood reservoir; vasoconstriction redirects perfusion and recruits stored blood toward central circulation.
distractors: Mucosal flow may decrease, risking ischaemia.
Extraction is not necessarily complete.
Severe or prolonged constriction can contribute to intestinal injury.

simulation.stem: An examination reveals raised JVP, a tender enlarged liver, ascites and ankle oedema. Which haemodynamic change unifies these?
options: High systemic venous pressure behind the right ventricle.
Reduced filtration from peripheral capillaries.
Increased pulmonary venous pressure without systemic congestion.
Reduced central venous pressure from depleted blood volume.
simulation.explanation: Right ventricular backward failure elevates right atrial and systemic venous pressures, causing jugular distension, hepatic congestion and dependent oedema.
distractors: Higher systemic venous pressure promotes, rather than reduces, filtration.
Isolated pulmonary venous congestion principally reflects left-sided failure.
Right-sided backward failure increases rather than decreases venous pressure.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 27 — Fetal Circulation and the Transition at Birth
simulation.stem: Immediately after the first effective breaths, what happens to pulmonary vascular resistance?
options: It rises because alveolar oxygen stimulates constriction.
It remains unchanged until umbilical vessels close.
It equals systemic resistance because both circuits merge.
It falls as the lungs expand and oxygen tension rises.
simulation.explanation: Lung aeration and increased alveolar oxygen rapidly lower pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing pulmonary blood flow.
distractors: Alveolar oxygen generally relieves pulmonary hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Pulmonary adaptation begins with the first breaths.
Pulmonary and systemic circuits retain very different resistance values.

simulation.stem: A technician places V1 at the fourth intercostal space. Where should the electrode be positioned horizontally?
options: At the left midclavicular line.
At the anterior axillary line.
At the right sternal border.
At the left midaxillary line.
simulation.explanation: V1 is positioned in the fourth intercostal space at the right edge of the sternum; V2 lies at the left sternal edge at the same level.
distractors: The left midclavicular line in the fifth space is the usual site of V4.
The anterior axillary position is used for V5.
The midaxillary position is used for V6.

simulation.stem: Which finding would most strongly suggest pulmonary rather than isolated dependent leg oedema?
options: Swelling that worsens around the ankles during standing.
Skin indentation remaining after pressing the ankle.
A unilateral swollen arm after mastectomy.
Lung crackles and dyspnoea with left-heart failure.
simulation.explanation: Left ventricular failure raises pulmonary venous pressure, causing lung interstitial and alveolar fluid with breathlessness and crackles.
distractors: Dependent leg oedema is more commonly systemic venous or local hydrostatic.
Pitting alone does not localise oedema to the lungs.
Postmastectomy swelling suggests lymphatic obstruction.

simulation.stem: Why can longstanding filarial lymphoedema become firm and poorly pitting?
options: Chronic protein-rich interstitial fluid promotes tissue fibrosis.
Ongoing rapid capillary reabsorption removes tissue proteins.
Longstanding venous dilation prevents connective-tissue changes.
A brief loss of arterial pressure causes permanent limb scarring.
simulation.explanation: Persistent failure of lymphatic drainage leaves protein-rich fluid in the interstitium, promoting chronic inflammation and fibrosis. This explains why longstanding lymphoedema becomes firm and often non-pitting.
distractors: Rapid reabsorption would tend to reduce swelling and protein accumulation.
Chronic interstitial protein deposition can drive fibrosis despite any venous tone changes.
The chronic fibrosis is linked to sustained lymphatic obstruction, not a brief arterial-pressure change.

simulation.stem: A patient with left-sided forward heart failure reports fatigue and produces very little urine. Which mechanism links the two?
options: Elevated venous pressure increases renal filtration.
Reduced systemic perfusion limits muscle and renal blood flow.
Pulmonary congestion causes systemic arteriolar dilation.
Increased left ventricular output stimulates renal water loss.
simulation.explanation: Reduced blood ejected from the left heart impairs delivery to skeletal muscle and kidneys, causing fatigue and oliguria.
distractors: Higher venous pressure does not directly improve GFR.
The primary forward mechanism is reduced output, not pulmonary congestion.
The syndrome involves reduced rather than excessive systemic delivery.

simulation.stem: A recording shows that cardiac vagal stimulation lowers the firing rate of the sinoatrial node. Which additional effect is expected?
options: Stronger ventricular contraction through beta-1 activation.
Faster impulse conduction through the AV node.
Slower impulse conduction through the AV node.
Faster pacemaker discharge through alpha-1 activation.
simulation.explanation: Parasympathetic acetylcholine acts at muscarinic M₂ receptors to slow both SA nodal firing and AV nodal conduction.
distractors: β₁ activation describes sympathetic, not vagal, stimulation.
AV conduction is slowed rather than accelerated by vagal action.
The major cardiac pacemaker effect is not mediated by α₁.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 8 — Measuring Cardiac Output and the Work of the Heart
simulation.stem: What conservation principle underlies Fick measurement of cardiac output?
options: Venous oxygen usually matches arterial oxygen content.
Oxygen consumption is independent of blood flow and extraction.
Oxygen use equals flow × arterial–venous oxygen difference.
The heart produces all consumed oxygen internally.
simulation.explanation: By mass balance, oxygen uptake across lungs and consumption by tissues equal cardiac output multiplied by arterial–venous oxygen content difference.
distractors: Tissues extract oxygen, so venous content is generally lower.
Extraction and flow together determine total oxygen consumption.
The body consumes oxygen but does not produce it.

simulation.stem: What keeps tissue fluid moving through collecting lymph vessels toward the great veins?
options: Valves, muscle movement and lymphatic contractions.
Direct diffusion of whole lymph vessels through tissues.
Constant backflow from the vena cava.
Only the left ventricular ejection pressure.
simulation.explanation: One-way valves, skeletal-muscle compression, respiratory movement and lymphatic smooth-muscle contraction promote forward flow. The valves prevent reflux between compressions, making the low-pressure pumping effective.
distractors: Whole vessels do not diffuse through tissues.
Backflow is limited by valves rather than required for transport.
Lymph flow is not driven directly by systemic arterial pressure.

simulation.stem: A patient with left-sided heart failure feels breathless when lying flat but improves after sitting up. Why?
options: Lying flat shifts peripheral blood toward congested lungs.
Lying flat reduces central blood volume.
Sitting up directly increases pulmonary capillary pressure.
Sitting up increases venous return from the legs.
simulation.explanation: Supine positioning returns peripheral blood to the thorax; a failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra flow, increasing pulmonary venous congestion.
distractors: Central thoracic volume commonly increases rather than decreases supine.
A higher pulmonary capillary pressure would worsen breathlessness.
Sitting upright tends to reduce thoracic venous return.

simulation.stem: A regular rhythm has 24 small squares between adjacent R waves at standard paper speed. Approximately what is the heart rate?
options: 50 beats/min.
80 beats/min.
63 beats/min.
60 beats/min.
simulation.explanation: The rate in a regular rhythm is 1500 divided by the R–R separation in small squares: 1500/24 = 62.5 beats/min, approximately 63.
distractors: 50 beats/min corresponds to about 30 small squares between R waves.
80 beats/min corresponds to about 18.75 small squares between R waves.
60 beats/min corresponds to about 25 small squares between R waves.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 11 — Arterial Pulse and Jugular Venous Pulse
simulation.stem: What is detected by the fingers when palpating the radial pulse?
options: A direct pulse of venous blood into the radial artery.
An arterial wall-distension pressure wave.
Individual red cells striking the wrist.
An electrical signal passing along the endothelium.
simulation.explanation: Each ventricular ejection creates an arterial pressure/distension wave that travels along the arteries. This pressure wave moves faster than the bulk blood itself.
distractors: Venous blood does not directly pulse into systemic arteries.
Red cells are not separately felt during palpation.
The palpable pulse is mechanical rather than an electrical conduction wave.

simulation.stem: V2 has been placed correctly and V4 is at its usual site. Where should V3 be attached?
options: At the fifth space, midaxillary line.
At the fifth space, anterior axillary line.
At the fourth space, right sternal border.
Halfway between the V2 and V4 electrodes.
simulation.explanation: V3 is placed between the already positioned V2 and V4, so the anatomical line between those contacts determines its location.
distractors: The midaxillary line at V4 level is used for V6.
The anterior axillary line at V4 level is used for V5.
The fourth right parasternal position belongs to V1.

simulation.stem: Where is the largest controllable fall in systemic vascular pressure normally produced?
options: Across the venae cavae.
Within the right atrium alone.
Across resistance arterioles.
Across large elastic arteries.
simulation.explanation: Small arteries and arterioles provide substantial resistance, producing a major pressure drop from arterial to capillary levels.
distractors: Large veins carry blood at low pressure and resistance.
Right atrial pressure is low but does not create the main distributed arterial drop.
Large elastic arteries conduct flow with relatively small resistance.

simulation.stem: Why does the sinoatrial node ordinarily set the heart's rhythm rather than latent pacemakers?
options: Its action potentials last longer than all other cells.
It has the fastest intrinsic depolarisation rate.
It receives oxygen from the pulmonary veins first.
Its cells have the largest ventricular muscle mass.
simulation.explanation: The SA node normally reaches threshold fastest and overdrive-suppresses slower latent pacemakers. Faster SA-node impulses normally suppress slower escape pacemakers.
distractors: Action potential duration is not the primary reason for the fastest spontaneous rate.
Coronary perfusion is not determined by pulmonary venous timing.
Pacemaker dominance does not depend on muscle mass.

simulation.chapter: Chapter 1 — Introduction to the Heart and Circulation
simulation.stem: Why can coordinated cardiac pumping continue without a new external nerve impulse for every beat?
options: The atrial myocardium conducts only during expiration.
Intrinsic pacemaker cells generate rhythmic impulses.
The sinoatrial node supplies the pressure needed for ejection.
Cardiac cells cannot spontaneously depolarise.
simulation.explanation: Specialised cardiac pacemaker cells depolarise spontaneously; autonomic nerves modulate rather than initiate each heartbeat.
distractors: Atrial conduction is not limited to expiration.
The SA node produces electrical impulses, not direct ejection pressure.
Some conducting cells possess spontaneous automaticity.

simulation.stem: A patient has near-normal resting cardiac output but very high ventricular filling pressures and pulmonary congestion. Which statement fits best?
options: Heart failure can occur with normal output.
High filling pressure proves adequate pumping.
Heart failure requires reduced ejection fraction.
Normal resting output excludes heart failure.
simulation.explanation: Heart failure includes states where output is maintained only at abnormally high filling pressures, causing congestion.
distractors: High filling pressures can be evidence of dysfunction rather than normality.
Diastolic failure can occur with preserved ejection fraction.
A near-normal output can be maintained at harmful filling pressures.

simulation.stem: Which pressure difference primarily drives blood back to the right atrium from the body?
options: Aortic systolic minus right ventricular systolic pressure.
Left ventricular systolic minus aortic diastolic pressure.
Systemic filling pressure minus right atrial pressure.
Pulmonary venous minus pulmonary capillary pressure.
simulation.explanation: Venous return depends on the upstream systemic filling pressure relative to right atrial pressure and the resistance to venous return.
distractors: Aortic-right ventricular systolic pressure is not the venous return driving gradient.
That difference is a pulse-pressure-related comparison.
Pulmonary venous pressure does not define systemic venous return.

simulation.stem: What can follow when the right ventricle fails to deliver adequate forward flow to the lungs?
options: Pulmonary flow rises despite low right ventricular output.
Less blood reaches the left heart for systemic output.
Systemic tissues receive more oxygen-rich blood immediately.
Left ventricular filling necessarily increases sharply.
simulation.explanation: Reduced right ventricular output limits pulmonary flow and subsequent return to the left atrium, compromising left-sided filling and delivery.
distractors: The right heart cannot deliver excess flow when severely failing.
Reduced pulmonary transit cannot raise systemic oxygen delivery.
Less pulmonary venous return tends to decrease left-sided filling.

It strengthens plasma oncotic pressure, reducing filtration.
It lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure, opposing filtration.
It strengthens the outward oncotic force favouring filtration.

Plasma protein concentration is held constant; the changed force is interstitial.
A change in interstitial protein does not directly lower capillary pressure.
